а.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic а, from Proto-Slavic *a ('and, whereas, but'), traced to a Proto-Indo-European pronominal ablative particle *h₁ōd ('from that, on the other hand'; compare Lithuanian õ 'and, whereas' and Sanskrit āt 'then, and').

history.meaning: from that, on the other hand

а.notes: Unlike и (which simply adds items together) and но (which states a direct contradiction), а contrasts two parallel facts or shifts the topic ('and as for...', 'whereas').

абсолютно.etymology: Adverb formed from абсолютный ('absolute, complete'), borrowed via German absolut or French absolu from Latin absolūtus ('freed, unrestricted, complete, unconditional'), the past participle of absolvere ('to loosen from, set free, complete').

аванс.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French avance ('advance payment; lead, step forward'), deverbal noun from avancer ('to move forward, advance'), from Vulgar Latin *abantiāre (from Late Latin abante 'in front, before', whence French avant).

history.meaning: in front → to advance → advance payment
advance payment (on wages or a contract)

авария.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (originally in maritime law as 'damage to a ship or cargo at sea') via Italian avaria, French avarie, or German Havarie, all from Arabic 'awāriyya ('damaged merchandise'), from 'awār ('defect, damage'). In 20th-century Russian the word broadened to any utility breakdown, pipe burst, or road accident.

автобус.etymology: Borrowed in the early twentieth century via French autobus / German Autobus, a blend of авто- ('automobile', from Ancient Greek αὐτός 'self') + -бус (clipped from омнибус, from Latin omnibus 'for all', dative plural of omnis).

автор.etymology: Borrowed via Polish autor and Byzantine/Medieval Latin pronunciation (where Latin au before a consonant was read av- under Greek influence) from Latin auctor ('originator, creator, author'), an agent noun from augeō ('to increase, originate, promote').

адвокат.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century) via German Advokat and Polish adwokat from Latin advocātus ('one called to aid a party in court, legal witness or counsel'), past participle of advocāre ('to summon, call to one's aid', from ad- 'to' + vocāre 'to call', from vōx 'voice').

history.meaning: to call to one's aid → legal counsel

администратор.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Administrator (or French administrateur) from Latin administrātor ('manager, steward, director'), derived from administrāre ('to manage, attend to, serve'), built on ad- + ministrāre ('to serve, attend', from minister).
администратор.notes: In Russian hotels, restaurants, and salons, **администратор** is the standard word for the front-desk receptionist or floor manager.

адрес.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French adresse ('direction of a letter, street address', originally 'straightening, directing toward') or German Adresse, from Old French adrecier ('to direct straight toward'), from Vulgar Latin *addīrectiāre (built on Latin dīrēctus 'straight, direct').

history.meaning: direction on a letter, street address

ай.etymology: Primary expressive interjection of sudden pain, fright, or surprise, inherited from Proto-Slavic *aj (and paralleled across Indo-European and other languages, compare German ei, French aïe, Sanskrit ē).

айфон.etymology: Borrowed in 2007 from English iPhone, the smartphone brand introduced by Apple Inc., coined from the prefix i- (originally standing for 'internet, individual, instruct, inform, inspire' in the 1998 iMac) + phone (short for telephone, from Ancient Greek φωνή 'voice, sound').

акварель.etymology: Borrowed from French aquarelle, from Italian acquerella ('watercolour'), a diminutive built on acqua 'water', from Latin aqua.
акварель.notes: In Russian акварель names both the paint medium (писать акварелью 'to paint in watercolour') and a finished watercolour picture.

акварельный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from акварель ('watercolour'), borrowed via French aquarelle from Italian acquerella (diminutive built on Latin aqua 'water').

акклиматизация.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French acclimatation / German Akklimatisation ('adaptation to a new climate or environment'), formed from the Latin prefix ad- ('to') + French climat ('climate', from Ancient Greek κλίμα klíma 'inclination of the earth toward the sun, latitude, climate') + -isation / -ация.

аккорд.etymology: Borrowed from French accord (and Italian accordo), from Vulgar Latin *accordare 'to bring into harmony, tune together', built on Latin ad- 'to' + cor 'heart'.

аккуратный.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German akkurat (or Polish akuratny) from Latin accūrātus ('done with care, exact, careful'), the past participle of accūrāre ('to take care of', from ad- + cūra 'care') + Russian adjectival suffix -ный.

алкоголь.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Alkohol or French alcool from Medieval Latin alcohol, originally borrowed from Arabic الْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, 'finely powdered antimony/kohl eye cosmetic obtained by sublimation'). Renaissance alchemists (notably Paracelsus) extended alcohol from 'any fine sublimated powder' to 'distilled spirit of wine' (alcohol vini).

history.meaning: sublimated essence → distilled spirit of wine

аллергия.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from German Allergie, coined in 1906 by the Viennese pediatrician Clemens von Pirquet from Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, 'other, different') + ἔργον (érgon, 'work, reaction'), literally 'altered reactivity' of the immune system.

алло.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century via French allô from English hallo / hello, the telephone greeting popularized by Thomas Edison in 1877 (originally an attention-calling shout of huntsmen and ferrymen).

анна.etymology: Borrowed via Byzantine Greek Ἄννα (Ánna) from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (Ḥannā), meaning 'grace, favour' (from the Semitic root ḥ-n-n 'to show favour, be gracious').

апельсин.etymology: Borrowed from Dutch appelsien, itself modelled on French pomme de Sine, literally 'apple from China', reflecting the sweet orange's trade route from East Asia to northern Europe.
апельсин.notes: Compare персик ('peach', originally 'Persian fruit') for another Russian fruit name preserving an old geographic origin.

апельсиновый.etymology: Formed in Russian with the relational suffix -овый from апельсин ('sweet orange'), which was borrowed in the Petrine era from Dutch appelsien (literally 'Chinese apple', calqued from French pomme de Sine, because sweet oranges were brought to Europe from China by Portuguese and Dutch traders).

history.meaning: orange (made of or flavoured with oranges)

аппетит.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via French appétit or German Appetit from Latin appetītus ('longing, desire, appetite for food'), derived from appetere ('to strive after, desire eagerly', from ad- + petere 'to seek, aim at').
аппетит.notes: Used in the standard mealtime wish **Приятного аппетита!** ('Bon appétit! / Enjoy your meal!').

арест.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German Arrest and Polish areszt from Medieval Latin arrestum ('seizure, detention by order of a court'), from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre ('to cause to stop, detain', from ad- 'to' + restāre 'to remain, stand back', whence also French arrêt).

арестовать.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via Polish aresztować and German arretieren / arrestieren from Medieval Latin arrestāre ('to stop, detain by legal authority'), formed in Russian with the verbal suffix -овать on арест ('arrest').

арка.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via Italian arca / arco, German Arke, or Polish arka from Latin arcus ('bow, vault, arch'). In Russian city architecture (especially in St Petersburg), арка often refers to the vaulted carriageway passage leading from the street into an inner courtyard (двор).

арочный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from арка ('arch', inserting a fleeting о and palatalizing к → ч before -н-), borrowed via Polish arka / German Arche or Italian arca from Latin arcus ('bow, arch').

morphemes.meaning: arch (арка, with fleeting о and к → ч)

архив.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century, originally feminine архива) via German Archiv and French archives from Late Latin archīum / archīvum ('public records office'), from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon, 'town hall, magistrate's residence where public records were kept'), derived from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, 'beginning, rule, magistracy').

балка.etymology: Borrowed via Polish belka / balka from Middle High German balke (modern German Balken, 'wooden beam, rafter, joist'), continuing Proto-Germanic *balkô (cognate with English balk and balcony).

балкон.etymology: Borrowed via French balcon from Italian balcone 'balcony, gallery', built on a Germanic word for a wooden beam or scaffold (*balko, akin to English balk and Russian балка 'beam').

балл.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French balle ('small ball, ballot ball'), used in voting and academic grading where white or black balls were dropped into an urn to score candidates; hence 'grade mark, score point, wind/earthquake force level'.

history.meaning: point, mark, score (in grading or competitions)

банк.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Bank (or French banque) from Italian banca / banco ('moneychanger's bench or counter table'), itself an early borrowing from Lombardic/Germanic *banki ('bench'). When a medieval Italian banker failed, his bench was broken (banca rotta, whence банкрот 'bankrupt').

history.meaning: moneychanger's table or bench → financial bank
bank (financial institution; pot in card games)

rootFamily.gloss: banquet (from the same Italian root banco 'bench')

банкет.etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th or early 18th century via German Bankett (and Polish bankiet) from French banquet ('feast, ceremonial dinner'), itself borrowed from Italian banchetto, a diminutive of banco ('bench, table'), originally referring to a light meal or snack eaten on a bench before coming to mean a grand formal dinner.

rootFamily.gloss: bank (from the same Italian root banco 'bench')

бар.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English bar ('counter across which drinks are served; pub, drinking establishment'), which comes from Old French barre ('barrier, rod, counter separating the server from patrons').

бармен.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English barman ('bartender'), a compound of bar ('tavern counter') and man.

барный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from бар ('bar, pub; drinks counter', borrowed from English bar).

history.meaning: bar → of a bar (e.g. барная стойка 'bar counter')

бархатный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from бархат ('velvet'), borrowed in late medieval Russian via Middle High German barchāt ('fustian, rich pile fabric'), ultimately from Arabic barrakān ('coarse camlet or heavy woven cloth').

батарея.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from French batterie ('artillery battery', originally 'a beating, bombardment', from battre 'to beat'). Because a cast-iron central-heating radiator is assembled from a row ('battery') of identical ribbed sections, Russian extended батарея (отопления) to mean a household heating radiator, as well as an electric battery.

history.meaning: artillery battery; row of linked units
artillery battery; electric battery; heating radiator

батарея.notes: In everyday Russian home life, **батарея** most often means a hot-water wall radiator (*тёплая батарея*).

батюшки.etymology: Exclamatory plural of батюшка ('dear father; village priest'), an affectionate derivative of батя ('father, dad', from Proto-Slavic *batja). Originally a shortened pious or startled invocation (such as Батюшки-святы! 'Holy fathers!'), now an everyday exclamation of surprise ('Goodness gracious!, Oh my!').

history.meaning: dear father → goodness gracious!, oh my!

башня.etymology: Developed from Old East Slavic башта, borrowed via Polish baszta or Czech bašta from Italian bastia 'fortified tower, bastion'. In Russian the ending was reshaped with the native place suffix -ня (as in пашня, таможня).

cognates.meaning: fortified projection (from the same Italian family)

башня.notes: Notice the fleeting vowel in the genitive plural: одна башня -> много башен.

беда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣда ('misfortune, calamity, need, compulsion'), from Proto-Slavic *běda (originally 'compulsion, distress', related to *běditi 'to compel, force', preserved in победить 'to conquer, overcome'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- ('to compel, urge, persuade'; cognate with Latin fīdō, Ancient Greek πείθω, and Gothic baidjan 'to compel').
беда.notes: The conversational reassurance **Не беда!** means 'No big deal! / Never mind!'.

бежать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣжати ('to run, flee'), from Proto-Slavic *běžati (stem *běg-), continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ- ('to flee, run'), directly cognate with Lithuanian bė́gti ('to run') and Ancient Greek φεύγω ('to flee', whence English fugitive).
бежать.notes: Alternates between **г** and **ж** in the present tense: **я бегу, они бегут**, but **ты бежишь, он бежит, мы бежим, вы бежите**.

без.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic безъ ('without'), from Proto-Slavic *bez, closely cognate with Lithuanian bè ('without'), Latvian bez, and Sanskrit bahíṣ ('outside').
без.notes: Always takes the genitive case: чай без сахара ('tea without sugar'), без десяти восемь ('ten to eight').

белый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣлъ / бѣлыи ('white, bright, shining'), from Proto-Slavic *bělъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰēlos ('shining, white', from *bʰel- 'to shine, flash'; compare Lithuanian bãltas 'white', Sanskrit bhāla 'brightness', and English bald, originally 'white-patched').

беременный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic беремяньныи ('pregnant', literally 'carrying a burden'), displaying East Slavic pleophony -ере- (compare Old Church Slavonic брѣменьнъ), derived from беремя ('load, burden, armful', standard Russian бремя 'burden'), from Proto-Slavic *bermę ('load, that which is borne'), from the PIE root *bʰer- ('to carry, bear'; cognate with English bear and birth).

history.meaning: burden, load → carrying a child, pregnant

rootFamily.gloss: to take (from the same PIE root *bʰer-)

беречь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic беречи (present берегу; showing East Slavic pleophony -ере-; compare Old Church Slavonic брѣщи), from Proto-Slavic *bergti ('to guard, care for, preserve'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- ('to keep safe, protect, hide'; cognate with German bergen 'to rescue, shelter').

history.meaning: to guard, treasure, take care of

бесплатный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prepositional phrase без платы ('without payment'), combining prefix бес- (voiceless variant of без- 'without' before п) + плата ('pay, fee', from Proto-Slavic *plata) + adjectival suffix -ный.

беспокоить.etymology: Formed in Russian from без покоя / беспокойный ('without peace/rest'), combining prefix бес- ('without', variant of без- before п) + покой ('peace, rest, quiet', from Proto-Slavic *pokojь) + verbal suffix -ить: literally 'to deprive someone of peace and quiet, disturb, bother'.

history.meaning: to deprive of rest → to bother, disturb, worry

беспорядок.etymology: Formed in Russian with the privative prefix без- / бес- ('without, lack of') and порядок ('order, sequence, tidy arrangement', derived from по- + ряд 'row, line, order', Proto-Slavic *rędъ).

history.meaning: lack of order, disorder, mess; (pl.) riots/disturbances

бечёвка.etymology: Formed with -ёвка from бечева ('towline, strong hauling rope used to pull river barges upstream'), which Vasmer traces as an early borrowing via Turkic from Persian پیچ (pēč 'twist, coil, cord').

бирка.etymology: Recorded in Russian first in the sense 'notched wooden tally stick used by tax collectors or herdsmen, trade tag'; Vasmer notes competing proposals, most often linking it either to an early Scandinavian borrowing (compare Old Swedish birk 'market jurisdiction/tally rule') or to regional Turkic/Tatar birkä ('tally mark').

history.meaning: luggage tag, price or garment label

благодарность.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ость from благодарный ('grateful, thankful'), built on Old Church Slavonic благодарити ('to thank, give thanks'), a loan-translation (calque) of Ancient Greek εὐχαριστέω (eukharistéō): благо- ('good', translating Greek εὖ-) + дарить / дар ('to give / gift', translating χάρις 'grace, favour, gift').

близкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic близькыи (extended with the adjectival suffix -к- from older близъ 'near'), from Proto-Slavic *blizъ / *blizъkъ ('near, close').

блин.etymology: Altered in Old East Slavic блинъ from earlier млинъ (with dissimilation of м-н > б-н; compare Ukrainian млинець), from Proto-Slavic *mlinъ ('pancake, flat cake made of ground flour'), derived from the root of молоть ('to grind grain in a mill', Proto-Slavic *melti, PIE *melh₂-). In modern colloquial Russian, блин! is also widely used as a minced oath ('damn! shoot!') substituting for a taboo profanity sharing the initial бл-.

history.meaning: to grind → batter cake made of ground meal

блюдо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic блюдо ('large platter, dish, course of food'), from Proto-Slavic *bľudo, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *biudaz / Gothic biups ('table, Wooden serving platter, dish', derived from *beudaną 'to offer, present at table', cognate with Old English bēod 'table, bowl' and English bid).

history.meaning: dish (both a serving platter and a prepared food course)

бог.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic богъ ('God'), from Proto-Slavic *bogъ (originally 'fortune, share, wealth' — still seen in богатый 'rich' and убогий 'poor' — and 'giver of good fortune, god'). Widely linked by Vasmer to Indo-Iranian *bhaga- (Sanskrit bhága 'dispenser, lord, fortune', Old Persian baga 'god') from PIE *bʰag- ('to apportion, share out').

history.meaning: good fortune; dispenser of fortune, god

бог.notes: Traditionally pronounced *бох* in the nominative singular (reflecting older spirant pronunciation of *г* in church vocabulary).

богатый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic богатыи (and Old Church Slavonic богатъ), from Proto-Slavic *bogatъ ('rich, wealthy, endowed by fortune'), formed with the suffix *-atъ from the archaic noun sense of *bogъ ('share, portion, wealth, good fortune', cognate with Sanskrit bhága- 'fortune, wealth, dispenser/lord' and Avestan baγa-; the same word that gave Бог 'God', originally 'giver of good fortune/shares').

бодрящий.etymology: Present active participle of бодрить ('to invigorate, brace, cheer up'), derived from бодрый ('vigorous, alert, brisk', from Old East Slavic бъдрыи and Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ, built on the same Indo-European root *bʰewdʰ- 'to be awake, alert' as будить 'to wake').

бокал.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French bocal or Italian boccale ('jug, goblet, drinking glass') from Late Latin baucālis, itself from Ancient Greek βαύκαλις (baúkalis, 'vessel for cooling wine or water').

болтать.etymology: Inherited East Slavic expressive/onomatopoeic verb (compare Ukrainian бовтати 'to stir, splash, chatter'), originally meaning 'to shake, stir, slosh liquid back and forth' (as in болтать ногами 'to dangle/swing one's legs' or болтунья 'scrambled eggs'). By metaphor ('wagging one's tongue'), болтать языком became the standard colloquial verb for 'to chatter, chat, blab'.

history.meaning: to stir, splash, swing back and forth
to swing, stir; to chat, chatter idly

больница.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic больница ('infirmary, hospital, house for the sick', attested in monastery rules from the 11th century), formed from больной ('sick, ill', from боль 'pain, illness') + the place/institution suffix -ница.

больно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from the neuter short form of больной ('painful, sore, sick'), derived from боль ('pain, ache'), from Proto-Slavic *bolь ('pain, sickness').

больше.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic больше ('more, bigger'), the neuter comparative degree of большой / великий, from Proto-Slavic *bolje / *boljьše ('more, larger').

большой.etymology: Developed in East Slavic from Old East Slavic большии, which was originally the comparative degree ('bigger, greater') of велии / великыи ('big, great'), from Proto-Slavic *boljьjь ('larger, stronger'; compare Sanskrit bála 'strength, power'). In Russian большой shifted from 'bigger' to the ordinary positive adjective 'big, large'.

борисовна.etymology: Russian feminine patronymic formed from the given name Борис (Old East Slavic Борисъ, attested since the 11th century from Bulgar Turkic Bogoris or as a short form of Борислав 'famous in battle') + possessive suffix -ов- + feminine patronymic suffix -на ('daughter of Boris').

ботинок.etymology: Formed in 19th-century Russian with the native singulative suffix -ок from French bottine ('ankle boot, half-boot'), itself a diminutive of botte ('boot').

брат.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic братъ (older братръ), from Proto-Slavic *bratrъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr ('brother') — one of the most stable kinship words across Indo-European languages, cognate with English brother, Latin frāter, and Sanskrit bhrātṛ.
брат.notes: Notice the irregular collective-origin plural: **братья**, genitive **братьев**.

брать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic брати (present беру, береши; Old Church Slavonic бьрати), from Proto-Slavic *bьrati ('to gather, take'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- ('to carry, bear, take'), directly cognate with English bear, Latin ferō, Ancient Greek φέρω, and Sanskrit bhárati.
брать.notes: Forms a classic suppletive aspect pair with perfective **взять** ('to take').

бронзовый.etymology: Relational and colour adjective formed with the suffix -овый from бронза ('bronze'), borrowed in the eighteenth century via French bronze / German Bronze from Italian bronzo ('bell metal, bronze', of contested Persian or Late Latin origin).

бронирование.etymology: Verbal noun in -ние formed from бронировать ('to reserve, book'), built in 20th-century Russian on броня / бронь ('official reservation, protected quota', originally 'armour, protective breastplate').

бронировать.etymology: Formed in 20th-century Russian with the verbal suffix -ировать from броня / бронь ('official protection, reserved quota, booking', which developed metaphorically from Old East Slavic броня 'armour, breastplate': securing a ticket or hotel room as if behind protective armour).

history.meaning: to secure a quota → to book, reserve

бронировать.notes: With stress on **-и́-** (**брони́ровать**), it means 'to book, reserve' (a hotel room or ticket); with stress on **-а́-** (**бронирова́ть**), it means 'to armour-plate'.

бронь.etymology: Formed in 20th-century Russian as a back-formation or clipped variant of броня ('official exemption, reserved quota, reservation'), which developed metaphorically from Old East Slavic броня ('coat of mail, armour', an early Slavic borrowing via Proto-Germanic *brunjǭ 'breastplate') — originally an 'armour-plated' ticket or official protection from requisitioning, then any hotel or ticket reservation.

бросать.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic бросати (originally 'to scrape, strip off, fling away'; compare Church Slavonic бръснути 'to shave, scrape' and Proto-Slavic *brъsati). In Russian its sense generalized from 'stripping or flinging off' to the everyday verb 'to throw, cast; to abandon'.

бросить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бросити, from Proto-Slavic *brositi ('to scrape off, strip, fling, throw'). Originally referring to stripping flax or scraping off bark/buds, in Russian it became the general perfective verb for 'to throw, fling' and figuratively 'to abandon, quit, leave someone'.

history.meaning: to throw; to quit; to leave/dump (someone)

брусок.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of брус ('squared timber beam, bar'), inherited from Old East Slavic брусъ and Proto-Slavic *brusъ ('squared beam; whetstone, block').

history.meaning: beam → small block, bar (of wood or stone), whetstone

буддийский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from буддизм / Будда ('Buddha'), borrowed from Sanskrit बुद्ध (Buddha, literally 'the Awakened One, the Enlightened One', past participle of budh- 'to awake, perceive, understand', cognate with Russian будить 'to wake up').

будильник.etymology: Formed in Russian (partially calquing German Wecker or French réveil) from будильный ('waking'), built on будить ('to wake someone up', from Old East Slavic будити, Proto-Slavic *buditi, the o-grade causative of *bъděti 'to be awake, keep watch', from PIE *bʰewdʰ- 'to be awake, aware') + the instrument suffix -ник.

будто.etymology: Univerbation in Middle Russian of будь то ('be it that, suppose that'), combining будь (the second-person singular imperative of быть 'to be') with the neuter demonstrative pronoun то ('that').

будущий.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бѫдѫщии ('that which will be, future'), the active participle formed from the future stem бѫд- / буд- ('will be', 1st sg. буду) of быти / быть ('to be', Proto-Slavic *bǫdǫ from PIE *bʰuH- with nasal infix).

history.meaning: future, next (and neuter noun будущее 'the future')

буква.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic букы (genitive букъве, plural букъви; Old Church Slavonic боукы, 'letter of the alphabet; beech tree'), from Proto-Slavic *buky, an early Slavic borrowing from Proto-Germanic *bōkō ('beech tree; carved beechwood rune-tablet, book', ancestor of English book and beech and German Buch / Buche). The modern nominative singular буква was rebuilt from the oblique stem букв-.

букет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French bouquet ('nosegay, bunch of flowers; aroma of wine'), originally a Norman-Picard dialectal diminutive of Old French bosc / bois ('wood, grove, little clump of trees').

history.meaning: little wood, clump of foliage → bunch of flowers; wine aroma

букинист.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French bouquiniste 'dealer in second-hand and antiquarian books', from bouquin 'old book', itself taken from Middle Dutch boeckin ('little book').
букинист.notes: Букинистический магазин is the standard Russian name for a second-hand or antiquarian bookshop.

букинистический.etymology: Adjective formed with -ический from букинист ('dealer in second-hand and antiquarian books'), borrowed from French bouquiniste, from bouquin ('old book'), which French borrowed from Middle Dutch boeckijn ('little book', diminutive of boec 'book').

cognates.meaning: book (same Germanic root as Dutch boec)

булочка.etymology: Formed in Russian as the affectionate diminutive (with suffix -очка) of булка ('white wheat roll or loaf'), borrowed via Polish bułka from Middle High German bulle or Latin bulla ('round swelling, bubble, round loaf').

булыжник.etymology: Formed with the suffix -ник from dialectal булыга ('rounded boulder, heavy lump of fieldstone, club'), an East Slavic word compared by Vasmer with Lithuanian bulis ('buttock, rounded mass') and Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- ('to swell, rounded object').

бульон.etymology: Borrowed from French bouillon 'broth', from bouillir 'to boil', which goes back to Latin bullire 'to bubble, boil' from bulla 'bubble'.
бульон.notes: Note how Russian spells the palatal French -ill- with льйо -> льо: бульон.

бумага.etymology: Recorded in Old Russian from the 14th century, first meaning 'cotton wool' (still seen in хлопчатобумажный 'cotton') and then 'rag paper'. Vasmer considers borrowing from Italian bambagia ('cotton', from Medieval Greek βάμβαξ, ultimately Persian pambak) the likeliest route.

бумажник.etymology: Formed in Russian from бумага ('paper; paper banknote') + the noun suffix -ник: originally a pocket case for carrying folded paper notes and documents, hence 'wallet'.

history.meaning: pocket wallet for notes and papers

morphemes.meaning: paper (from бумага with г -> ж alternation)

бумажный.etymology: Formed in Russian from бумага ('paper', historically 'cotton, rag paper' in 14th-century Old Russian, borrowed from Italian bambagia 'cotton') + the adjectival suffix -ный (with regular palatal alternation г → ж).

бурый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic буръ ('dark brown, greyish-brown'), cited by Vasmer either as an early borrowing from Turkic bur ('fox-colored, reddish-brown') or via Persia from Proto-Indo-European *bher- ('dark, brown').

буря.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic буря ('storm, tempest'), from Proto-Slavic *burja, from Proto-Indo-European *bheur- ('to boil, seethe, rage').

бутафорский.etymology: Derived in Russian with the adjective suffix -ский from бутафория / бутафор ('stage prop maker'), borrowed from Italian buttafuori ('stage manager, prop handler', literally 'throw outside', from buttare 'to throw' + fuori 'outside').

бутерброд.etymology: Borrowed from German Butterbrot, 'bread and butter', a compound of Butter 'butter' and Brot 'bread'. In Russian the word widened to any open sandwich, so a бутерброд can carry cheese or sausage and no butter at all.
бутерброд.notes: A sandwich made of two slices is often called сэндвич; бутерброд is usually open.

бутик.etymology: Colloquial Russian clipping of бутерброд ('open sandwich') suffixed with the diminutive -ик, shaped playfully as a homonym of бутик ('boutique'); бутерброд itself was borrowed from German Butterbrot ('buttered bread').

бутылка.etymology: Formed in Early Modern Russian (attested from 1695 in the Petrine era) with the native suffix -ка from бутыль ('large glass bottle, carboy'), borrowed via Polish butelka / butla from French bouteille ('bottle'), which goes back to Late Latin buticula ('small wine-skin or flask').

буфетчик.etymology: Formed in Russian from буфет ('sideboard, refreshment counter, buffet') + the agent suffix -чик; буфет was borrowed in the 18th century from French buffet.

буханка.etymology: Formed with -ка from dialectal бухон 'round loaf', borrowed via Polish bochen 'loaf of bread' and Old High German fohhenza, ultimately going back to Latin focacium 'hearth-baked bread' (from focus 'hearth', the same Latin source as Italian focaccia).

буше.etymology: Borrowed from French bouchée ('mouthful; small filled pastry or sponge cake'), a derivative of bouche ('mouth'), from Latin bucca ('cheek, mouth').

бывшая.etymology: Substantivized feminine form of бывший ('former, past'), historically the past active participle of быть ('to be'), from Proto-Slavic *byti, from Proto-Indo-European *bheuH- ('to become, be').

бывший.etymology: Lexicalized past active participle of быть ('to be', Old East Slavic быти, Proto-Slavic *byti, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- 'to become, grow, be'). From its literal participial sense 'having been', it became the standard adjective for 'former, ex-'.

быстрее.etymology: Comparative degree formed with the productive comparative suffix -ее from быстрый ('fast, quick, swift', from Old East Slavic быстръ, Proto-Slavic *bystrъ).

быстренько.etymology: Colloquial adverb formed from быстренький, the affectionate diminutive (with suffix -еньк-) of быстрый ('fast, quick'), from Proto-Slavic *bystrъ ('swift, clear, sharp').

быстро.etymology: Adverb formed from the short neuter of быстрый ('fast, swift, rapid'), inherited from Old East Slavic быстръ ('swift-flowing, keen, quick'), from Proto-Slavic *bystrъ.

быстрый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic быстръ / быстрыи ('swift-flowing, rapid, keen'), from Proto-Slavic *bystrъ (originally applied to rushing mountain streams, with an epenthetic -t- inserted in the cluster -sr- from an older root *bys-rъ 'gushing, rushing'; compare Old Norse bysia 'to gush forth').

быть.etymology: Быть is an inherited Slavic verb. Vasmer compares Lithuanian būti and older Indo-European words for being, becoming and coming into existence. That older family helps explain why the history of this everyday verb reaches beyond the modern English gloss to be.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: быть

бюллетень.etymology: Borrowed from French bulletin ('official report, ballot slip'), from Italian bullettino ('official note, pass'), diminutive of bulletta / bulla, from Medieval Latin bulla ('sealed document, papal bull'). In Soviet and modern Russian also used for a medical sick-leave certificate.

бюро.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries from French bureau ('writing desk; office, agency'), originally Old French burel ('coarse woollen baize cloth used to cover writing tables', then the writing table itself, and finally the office room where clerks worked). Indeclinable in Russian (e.g. бюро находок 'lost-and-found office').

в.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въ, from Proto-Slavic *vъ(n) ('in, into'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₁en ('in') with a prosthetic labial glide *v- added before the reduced vowel. Its original final nasal *-n survives in combinations with third-person pronouns (в нём, в него) and in older compounds such as внутрь.
в.notes: Takes the prepositional case for static location (в комнате) and the accusative case for motion into a place (в комнату); becomes во before certain consonant clusters (во дворе).

в-третьих.etymology: Parenthetical adverbial formed from the preposition в ('in') + the locative plural of третий ('third'), from Proto-Slavic *tretьjь ('third'), from Proto-Indo-European *tritjos.

вагон.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via French wagon or German Waggon from English waggon / wagon ('wheeled cart, railway car'), itself from Dutch wagen, from Proto-Germanic *wagnaz ('wagon').

вакцина.etymology: Borrowed via French vaccine or scientific New Latin vaccina from Latin vaccinus ('relating to cows', from vacca 'cow'), coined by Edward Jenner in 1798 for cowpox inoculation against smallpox.

валенок.etymology: Singular back-formation with -ок from plural валенки ('felted wool boots'), derived from the passive participle валеный of валять ('to full, felt wool, roll'), from Proto-Slavic *valjati.

валет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French valet ('page, squire, knave in playing cards'), from Old French vaslet / varlet ('young nobleman, squire'), from Medieval Latin vassellittus, diminutive of vassallus ('vassal').

вальс.etymology: Borrowed from French valse, which in turn comes from German Walzer, a noun from walzen 'to turn, to roll'. The dance is named for its turning steps.

валять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic валяти ('to roll, tumble'), from Proto-Slavic *valjati, an iterative-causative verb related to *valiti ('to roll, throw down'), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- ('to turn, roll').

history.meaning: to roll, felt; to play the fool (валять дурака)

валяться.etymology: Reflexive and middle-voice form of валять ('to roll, toss about') with the suffix -ся, from Proto-Slavic *valjati sę ('to roll oneself, lie scattered around').

вампир.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via Western European languages (German Vampir, French vampire) from Serbian вампир, descending from Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrь ('vampire, revenant', compare native Russian упырь).

ванильный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from ваниль ('vanilla'), borrowed via French vanille and German Vanille from Spanish vainilla ('vanilla pod', literally 'little sheath'), diminutive of vaina from Latin vagina ('sheath, pod').

ванная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from ванная комната ('bath room'), derived from ванна ('bathtub'), which was borrowed in the 18th century from German Wanne ('tub, bath', originally 'winnowing basket', from Latin vannus).
ванная.notes: Declines like a feminine adjective (**в ванной**, **из ванной**); the bathtub itself is the noun **ванна**.

варвар.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic варъваръ from Byzantine Greek βάρβαρος (várvaros, earlier bárbaros, 'foreigner, non-Greek'), an onomatopoeic reduplication imitating unintelligible foreign speech ('bar-bar').

варварство.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ство from варвар ('barbarian'), ultimately from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος ('non-Greek, foreigner').

варенье.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic варение ('boiling, cooked dish, fruit preserves'), a verbal noun from варить ('to boil, cook', from Proto-Slavic *variti, causative of *vьrěti 'to bubble, boil', from PIE *wer- 'to burn, be hot'). In Russian cuisine варенье specifically names whole-berry or fruit preserves boiled in sugar syrup.

history.meaning: to boil, cook → boiled dish, preserves

вариант.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Variante or French variante from Latin variāns (genitive variantis, 'varying, differing'), present participle of variāre ('to vary, change, diversify'), from varius ('varied, diverse').

варёный.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of варить ('to boil, cook'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *variti ('to boil, cook'), causative of *vьrěti ('to boil, bubble'), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- ('to burn, heat').

ваш.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вашь (f. ваша, n. ваше), from Proto-Slavic *vašь ('your, yours [plural]'), formed from the second-person plural oblique pronoun stem *va- / *vo- (seen in вас, вам; compare Latin vōs 'you') + possessive suffix *-sjь.

вбить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from в- ('into') + бить ('to beat, strike'), from Proto-Slavic *vъbiti ('to drive in, hammer in'), from *biti ('to strike').

history.meaning: to hammer in; to enter into a bill

вверх.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic directional phrase въ вьрхъ ('into the top, upward'), combining the preposition в ('into') with the accusative singular of верх ('top, upper part', from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ).

вверху.etymology: Adverb formed in East Slavic by fusing the preposition в ('in, at') with верху (locative singular in -у of верх 'top, upper part', from Old East Slavic вьрхъ and Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ).

ввести.etymology: Borrowed or shaped via Old Church Slavonic въвести (and inherited Old East Slavic въвести), from в- ('in, into') + вести ('to lead'), from Proto-Slavic *vesti ('to lead').

ввинтить.etymology: Formed with the prefix в- ('in, into') + винтить ('to screw'), a denominative verb from винт ('screw, spiral thread'), which entered Russian via Polish gwint from Early New High German Gewinde ('spiral thread, winding, screw', from winden 'to wind, twist').

history.meaning: screw → to screw in, bolt in

вводить.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of ввести, formed from в- ('in, into') + водить ('to lead', iterative of вести), from Proto-Slavic *vъvoditi ('to lead in, bring in').

вводиться.etymology: Passive and reflexive derivative of вводить ('to introduce, bring in') formed with the postfix -ся, from в- + водить + -ся.

вдвое.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в двое ('into two, twofold'), combining the preposition в with двое ('two, a pair', collective numeral from Proto-Slavic *dъvoje, built on два 'two').

history.meaning: in two, twice as much, twofold

вдох.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from вдохнуть ('to breathe in, inhale'), built from prefix в- ('in') + дохнуть / дышать ('to breathe', from Proto-Slavic *dъxnǫti, with strong yer ъ vocalized to о in вдох; from the same root as дух 'breath, spirit' and воздух 'air').

вдыхать.etymology: Imperfective verb paired with вдохнуть ('to inhale, breathe in'), formed with prefix в- ('in') + дыхать ('to breathe', iterative stem of дышать / дохнуть, from Proto-Slavic *dyxati, related by lengthened ablaut to дух 'breath, spirit').

вегетарианский.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ский from вегетарианец ('vegetarian'), borrowed in the late 19th century from English vegetarian (coined in the 1840s from vegetable + -arian, ultimately from Late Latin vegetabilis 'animating, growing').

ведомо.etymology: Surviving mainly in the phrase без ведома ('without someone's knowledge'), originally the neuter singular present passive participle вѣдомо ('known') of вѣдати ('to know'), from Proto-Slavic *věděti ('to know'), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- ('to see, know').

ведущий.etymology: Substantivized and adjectival present active participle of вести ('to lead, conduct'), from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic ведущии, from Proto-Slavic *vedǫtji ('leading').

ведь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣдь, originally a shortened form of the ancient perfect/present verb вѣдѣ ('I know') or imperative вѣждь ('know!'), from Old East Slavic вѣдѣти ('to know', Proto-Slavic *věděti). It grammaticalized into a conversational discourse particle meaning 'after all, as you know, you see'.

вежливость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from вежливый ('polite, courteous'), which derives from Old Russian вѣжа ('one who knows customs and manners'), from вѣдати ('to know', Proto-Slavic *věděti).

вежливый.etymology: Developed from Old Russian вѣжливыи ('knowing how to behave, courteous, well-mannered'), derived from older вѣжа ('one who knows customs, an expert', the positive counterpart of modern невежа 'boor, ignorant person'), built on the Old East Slavic verb вѣдати ('to know', from Proto-Slavic *věděti, PIE *weyd- 'to see, know'; cognate with English wit and wise).

history.meaning: to know → one who knows proper custom

везде.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьсьде ('everywhere', Old Church Slavonic вьсьде), from Proto-Slavic *vьsьde, compounded from the stem of весь ('all, every', Proto-Slavic *vьsь) + the locative adverbial suffix *-de (seen in где 'where' and здесь 'here'), with regular voicing сд > зд after loss of the weak yer.

morphemes.meaning: all, every (from вьсь, with с → з before д)

велеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic велѣти ('to command, wish'), from Proto-Slavic *velěti ('to wish, command'), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- ('to choose, wish'; cognate with Latin velle and English will).

великий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic великыи (and Old Church Slavonic великъ, extended with -ик- from older вель / велии 'great'), from Proto-Slavic *velikъ ('great, large').
великий.notes: In modern Russian, the long form **великий** means 'great, eminent' (Пётр Великий), whereas the short form **велик / велика / велики** means 'too big (in clothing/shoe size)' (*костюм мне велик*).

великоватый.etymology: Formed with the attenuative suffix -оват- ('somewhat, slightly too') from великий ('big, great; too large in short forms велик'), from Proto-Slavic *velikъ ('big, great').

великодушно.etymology: Adverb derived from великодушный ('magnanimous, generous'), an Old Church Slavonic calque (великодушьнъ) of Greek μεγαλόψυχος (megalópsychos, 'great-souled'), from великий ('great') + душа ('soul').

великолепие.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic великолѣпиѥ ('magnificence, splendor'), a calque of Greek μεγαλοπρέπεια (megaloprépeia, 'befitting a great person, magnificence'), from великий ('great') + лѣпыи ('fitting, beautiful').

великолепный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic великолѣпьнъ ('magnificently fitting, majestic, splendid'), a calque of Ancient Greek μεγαλοπρεπής (megaloprepḗs, 'befitting a great person, magnificent'), compounded from великъ ('great') + лѣпъ ('fitting, comely, beautiful', from Proto-Slavic *lěpъ, preserved in нелепый 'absurd, unfitting' and Ukrainian ліпий / гарний).

величество.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic величьство ('greatness, majesty'), formed from великий ('great', Proto-Slavic *velikъ) + abstract suffix -ьство, later used as a translation of Latin maiestas ('Majesty') in royal titles.

венец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣньць and reinforced by Old Church Slavonic вѣньць ('wreath, crown'), diminutive of Proto-Slavic *věnъ ('braided wreath, garland'), from *viti ('to twist, weave', PIE *weh₁y-).

веник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣникъ ('bundle of leafy twigs, besom broom'), from Proto-Slavic *věnikъ, derived from *věnъ ('bundle, wreath'), from *viti ('to plait, bind').

венок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣнъкъ ('garland, wreath'), a diminutive with suffix -ок of Proto-Slavic *věnъ ('braided wreath'), from the root of *viti ('to weave, plait').

вентиль.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries from German Ventil ('valve, tap, shut-off cock'), from Medieval Latin ventīle ('sluice gate, air-vent'), derived from Latin ventus ('wind, air').

вентилятор.etymology: Borrowed via German Ventilator from Latin ventilator 'winnower, airer', an agent noun from ventilare 'to fan, wave in the air', itself built on ventus 'wind'.

вентиляция.etymology: Borrowed via German Ventilation or French ventilation from Latin ventilatio ('an airing, winnowing'), from ventilare ('to fan, air, winnow'), derived from ventus ('wind').

венчик.etymology: Diminutive of венец ('crown, rim') or веник ('twig broom, whisk') formed with the suffix -чик, used in culinary Russian for a wire whisk (originally a bundle of peeled twigs used for whipping).

вера.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣра ('faith, trust, oath'), from Proto-Slavic *věra ('faith, belief'), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ro- ('true, trustworthy'; cognate with Latin verus 'true' and German wahr).

веранда.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via English veranda and French véranda from Hindi varanda / Bengali baranda, itself borrowed from Portuguese varanda ('railing, balcony, terrace').

верить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣрити ('to believe, trust'), a denominative verb formed from вѣра ('faith, belief, trust'), from Proto-Slavic *věra (related to Latin vērus 'true' and German wahr 'true', from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ro-).

вериться.etymology: Impersonal reflexive verb formed with -ся from верить ('to believe'), from Old East Slavic вѣрити ('to believe, trust'), derived from вѣра ('faith, belief', Proto-Slavic *věra).

верность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from верный ('faithful, loyal, true'), from Old East Slavic вѣрьныи, derived from вѣра ('faith, trust', Proto-Slavic *věra).

вернуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьрнути ('to turn back, give back, return'), formed with the semelfactive/perfective suffix -нуть (with simplification of *rtn > рн) from the Proto-Slavic root *vьrtěti ('to turn', modern Russian вертеть, from PIE *wert- 'to turn'; cognate with Latin vertō).

верный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣрьныи (and Old Church Slavonic вѣрьнъ 'faithful, true, trustworthy'), formed with the suffix -ный from вѣра ('faith, trust, truth'), from Proto-Slavic *věra (cognate with Latin vērus 'true' and German wahr 'true').

верхний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьрхьнии ('upper, top'), derived from верх ('top, summit, upper part', from Old East Slavic вьрхъ, Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ, cognate with Lithuanian viršùs 'top, peak') + the spatial adjectival suffix -ний.

верхушка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the suffix -ушка from верх ('top, upper part, summit'), inherited from Old East Slavic вьрхъ and Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ.

history.meaning: top → very top, tip, crown (of a tree or pastry)

вершина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьршина ('top, summit'), formed with the singulative/locative suffix -ина from вьрхъ (modern верх, 'top, upper part'), from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ ('peak, top').

вершить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьршити ('to top off a stack, bring to completion, decide'), denominative verb from вьрхъ (верх, 'top, summit', Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ).

верёвка.etymology: Diminutive-type derivative of dialectal and Old East Slavic вервь ('cord, measuring rope'), from Proto-Slavic *vьrvь ('rope, cord'), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- ('to turn, twist, bind').

вес.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣсъ ('weight, balance scale'), from Proto-Slavic *věsъ ('weight, hanging'), avrddhi-grade noun from the root of *visěti ('to hang') and *věsiti ('to hang, weigh').

весенний.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ний from весна ('spring', inserting a fleeting е in the stem весн-), inherited from Old East Slavic весна and Proto-Slavic *vesna ('spring', from Proto-Indo-European *wésr̥, cognate with Latin vēr and Lithuanian vasara 'summer').

весть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣсть ('news, Tidings, report'), from Proto-Slavic *věstь ('knowledge, message'), formed from *věd-ti (the root of *věděti 'to know', PIE *weyd-).

весь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьсь (f. вься, n. вьсе, pl. вьси), from Proto-Slavic *vьxъ / *vьśь ('all, the whole'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *wih₁so- ('all, whole'; cognate with Lithuanian vìsas 'all' and Sanskrit víśva 'every, all').

весьма.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вьсьма ('completely, altogether, very'), an archaic instrumental form built on вьсь (весь, 'all, whole', Proto-Slavic *vьxъ / *vьsь).

весёлый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic веселыи (and Old Church Slavonic веселъ 'merry, joyful, glad'), from Proto-Slavic *veselъ ('joyful, merry'), with close Baltic cognates (Latvian vesels 'healthy, whole, hale'). The semantic shift between 'healthy, hale, vigorous' (Baltic) and 'merry, cheerful' (Slavic) is an ancient Balto-Slavic development.

ветчина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ветъшина ('cured or aged meat, ham', attested in the 16th-century Domostroi), formed with the meat-designation suffix -ина (as in свинина, говядина, баранина) from ветхий ('old, aged', Old East Slavic ветъхъ, Proto-Slavic *vetъxъ 'old', cognate with Latin vetus 'old'), with dissimilation of -тш- > -тч-. Originally ветчина meant 'aged/cured salted pork' as opposed to fresh pork (свежина).

вечер.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вечеръ, from Proto-Slavic *večerъ, closely cognate with Lithuanian vãkaras and Latvian vakars ('evening'), and compared by Vasmer with Latin vesper and Ancient Greek ἕσπερος.

вечеринка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the compound suffix -инка (diminutive of dialectal/archaic вечерина 'evening gathering') from вечер ('evening', Old East Slavic вечеръ, Proto-Slavic *večerъ).

вечерний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вечернии ('of the evening'), formed from вечер ('evening', from Proto-Slavic *večerъ) + the temporal adjectival suffix -ний.

вечером.etymology: Lexicalized instrumental singular of вечер ('evening'), used adverbially to express time when ('in the evening'). Inherited from Old East Slavic вечеръ, from Proto-Slavic *večerъ (compare Lithuanian vãkaras 'evening').

вечность.etymology: Derived with the abstract noun suffix -ость from вечный ('eternal'), from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic вѣчьныи, derived from вѣкъ (век, 'age, lifetime, eternity', Proto-Slavic *věkъ).

вешалка.etymology: Formed with the instrument/place suffix -лка from вешать ('to hang up'), iterative of весить ('to hang'), from Proto-Slavic *věšati ('to hang repeatedly').

вешаться.etymology: Reflexive form of вешать ('to hang') with the suffix -ся, from Proto-Slavic *věšati sę ('to hang oneself, cling to someone').

history.meaning: to hang oneself; to throw oneself at someone

вещдок.etymology: 20th-century Russian legal and police syllabic abbreviation of вещественное доказательство ('material/physical evidence'), combining вещественный ('material, physical', from вещь 'thing') and доказательство ('proof, evidence').

вещество.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вещьство ('nature, essence, substance'), formed from вещь ('thing, matter', Proto-Slavic *vektь) + abstract suffix -ьство, used as a calque of Greek οὐσία and Latin substantia.

вещичка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive of вещь ('thing, item') formed via вещица + suffix -ка; вещь comes from Old Church Slavonic вещь ('thing, matter'), from Proto-Slavic *vektь.

взаимно.etymology: Adverb derived from взаимный ('mutual, reciprocal'), built on the older phrase въ заимъ ('on loan, in exchange'), from заимъ / заём ('loan, taking in turn', from за- + ять / иметь 'to take').

взаимность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from взаимный ('mutual, reciprocal'), from the historical phrase въ заимъ ('in exchange, reciprocally').

взаимовыгодный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from взаимно / взаимо- ('mutually') + выгодный ('profitable, advantageous', from выгода 'benefit, profit').

взаймы.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в займы (accusative plural of заём, Old East Slavic заимъ 'loan'), formed from за- + *jęti ('to take', Proto-Slavic *zaiti / *zajьmъ).

взбесить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('up, into an intense state') + бесить ('to madden, enrage'), which derives from бес ('demon, evil spirit', Proto-Slavic *běsъ).

history.meaning: to infuriate, drive into a rage

взбить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('upward') + бить ('to beat, strike', Proto-Slavic *biti), literally 'to beat up into a froth or fluff'.

history.meaning: to whip, beat (eggs, cream), fluff up

взбодрить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('up') + бодрить ('to invigorate, cheer up'), from бодрый ('brisk, cheerful, alert', Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ 'watchful, awake').

взбодриться.etymology: Reflexive form of взбодрить ('to perk up, invigorate') with the suffix -ся, built on вз- + бодрить (from бодрый 'vigorous, alert', Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ).

взвешивать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ива- from взвесить ('to weigh'), from вз- ('up, lifting on scales') + весить ('to weigh, hang', from вес 'weight', Proto-Slavic *věsъ).

взглянуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb in -нуть formed from взглядывать ('to cast a glance upward or at something'), built on prefix вз- ('up, suddenly') + глядеть ('to look, gaze', from Proto-Slavic *ględati).

history.meaning: to cast a glance, take a quick look

взлететь.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('upward') + лететь ('to fly', Proto-Slavic *letěti), literally 'to fly up, take off'.

взлом.etymology: Deverbal action noun from взломать ('to break open'), formed from вз- ('up, open') + лом ('breaking', from ломать 'to break', Proto-Slavic *lomiti).

взломать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('up, open by force') + ломать ('to break', Proto-Slavic *lamati / *lomiti), meaning to prize open a lock or door, and in modern usage to crack or hack a system.

взрослеть.etymology: Inchoative verb formed with the suffix -еть ('to become') from взрослый ('grown-up, adult'), historically a past participle derived from взрасти / взрости ('to grow up', from вз- + расти).

взрослый.etymology: Formed from the past active participle or verbal adjective of взрасти / взросло ('to grow up'), built from the upward prefix вз- ('up') + рос- (the past-tense stem of расти 'to grow', from Proto-Slavic *orsti) + -лый. Functions both as an adjective ('adult, grown-up') and as a substantivized noun ('an adult').

взрыв.etymology: Deverbal noun from взорвать / взрывать ('to blow up, tear up from underneath'), formed from вз- ('upward') + рыть ('to dig, tear', or рвать 'to tear', conflated in East Slavic *vъzryvati).

взятка.etymology: Formed in Russian from взять ('to take', from Old East Slavic възяти, a compound of въз- + яти 'to take') with the noun suffix -ка. Originally meaning simply 'that which is taken, a levy, exaction, or trick in cards', it specialized in administrative and everyday usage to mean an illicit payment or 'bribe'.

взяточник.etymology: Formed in Russian with the agent suffix -ник from взятка ('bribe', with stem alternation к > ч before -ник), itself derived from взять ('to take', Old East Slavic възяти).

взять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic възяти (future возьму, past взял; Old Church Slavonic възѧти), from Proto-Slavic *vъzęti ('to take up, pick up'), formed from prefix *vъz- ('up') + *jęti ('to take, grasp', from PIE *h₁em- 'to take'; compare занять 'to occupy' and принять 'to accept'). Serves as the suppletive perfective partner of брать.
взять.notes: Future tense vocalizes the historical yer vowel of the prefix *въз-*: **я возьму, ты возьмёшь, они возьмут**.

вид.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic видъ and Old Church Slavonic видъ ('sight, look, appearance, form, species'), from Proto-Slavic *vidъ, built on the Indo-European visual root *weyd- ('to see, know', cognate with видеть 'to see' and Latin vidēre).

видео.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English video, which was coined in television technology in the 1930s (as a counterpart to audio) from Latin videō ('I see'), first-person singular present of vidēre ('to see', cognate with Russian видеть).

history.meaning: I see → television/visual signal and recording

видеозапись.etymology: 20th-century compound of видео- (from English video, from Latin video 'I see') + запись ('recording, entry', deverbal noun from записать 'to write down, record').

видеонаблюдение.etymology: Modern compound combining видео- ('video', from Latin video 'I see') + наблюдение ('observation, surveillance', from наблюдать 'to watch, observe').

видеорегистратор.etymology: Modern compound of видео- ('video', from Latin video) + регистратор ('recorder, registrar', from Medieval Latin registrator, from regerere 'to record').

видимость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from видимый ('visible', originally the present passive participle of видеть 'to see', Proto-Slavic *viděti).

видный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from вид ('view, appearance, sight'), from Proto-Slavic *vidъ ('sight, look'), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- ('to see').

визитка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation with suffix -ка of визитная карточка ('visiting card, business card'), from визит ('visit'), borrowed from French visite (from visiter, Latin visitare 'to go to see').

викин.etymology: Possessive adjective formed with the suffix -ин from Вика, the standard Russian hypocoristic short form of the female given name Виктория (from Latin Victoria, 'victory').

вилка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of вилы ('pitchfork'), inherited from Old East Slavic вила / вилы ('forked branch, pitchfork') and Proto-Slavic *vila ('fork', originally something twisted or branching in two, related to вить 'to twist, wind'). When the table fork entered Russian dining, the diminutive вилка became its everyday name.

вилла.etymology: Borrowed via Italian villa (or German Villa) from Latin vīlla ('country house, estate, farmstead'), related to vīcus ('village, group of houses').

винный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic виньныи ('relating to wine'), formed with the adjective suffix -ный from вино ('wine'), borrowed in Proto-Slavic (*vino) from Gothic or Latin vinum.

вино.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вино (and Old Church Slavonic вино), borrowed in the Proto-Slavic period (*vino) via Gothic wein or directly from Latin vīnum ('wine'), an ancient Mediterranean wanderword shared with Ancient Greek οἶνος (oînos).

виноватый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic виноватыи ('guilty, at fault, to blame'), formed with the suffix -оватый from вина ('fault, guilt, blame, cause', from Proto-Slavic *vina, cognate with Lithuanian vainà 'fault, blame').

виновный.etymology: Derived via виновный / виноватый from вина ('fault, guilt, cause'), inherited from Old East Slavic вина ('cause, blame, guilt'), from Proto-Slavic *vina.

виноградник.etymology: Formed with the place suffix -ник from виноград ('grapes, grapevines'), from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic виноградъ ('vineyard, grapevine'), a Gothic borrowing (*weinagards 'wine-garden').

винотека.etymology: Borrowed from Italian vinoteca or formed internationally from вино ('wine', Latin vinum) + -тека ('collection, repository', from Ancient Greek θήκη thḗkē 'case, repository').

history.meaning: wine collection, wine cellar or boutique

винт.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via Polish gwint ('screw thread, screw') from Early Modern High German Gewinde ('spiral thread, winding, screw'), a collective noun from winden ('to wind, twist', cognate with English wind).

вирус.etymology: Borrowed via Western European scientific usage from Latin virus ('slimy liquid, poison, venom'), from Proto-Indo-European *weys- ('poison, slime').

висеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic висѣти (present вишу, висит), from Proto-Slavic *visěti ('to hang, be suspended'), an intransitive stative verb in *-ěti related to transitive вешать ('to hang something up').

виски.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English whisky / whiskey, itself an anglicization of Scottish Gaelic uisge-beatha and Irish uisce beatha ('water of life', a calque of Medieval Latin aqua vītae; compare the parallel formation of Russian водка from вода 'water').

вкладывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ыва- from вкласть / вкладывать ('to put in, lay in, invest'), from в- ('in, into') + класть ('to lay, put', Proto-Slavic *klasti).

включать.etymology: Imperfective partner of включить ('to include, insert into a circuit, turn on'), formed from prefix в- ('in, into') + ключ ('key, clasp, switch', from Proto-Slavic *kľučь). Originally 'to lock or clasp into a whole ('include')', and from the era of electrical engineering 'to close a switch into the circuit, turn on (a light or appliance)'.

history.meaning: to include; to switch on, turn on (imperfective)

включить.etymology: Formed from prefix в- ('in, into') + ключить (built on ключ 'key, bolt, switch', from Proto-Slavic *kľučь). First meant 'to enclose, include in a list or bill', and in the late 19th–20th centuries acquired the technical and everyday sense 'to engage a valve or electrical switch, turn on'.

history.meaning: to include; to turn on (light, water, heating)

вколоть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from в- ('into') + колоть ('to prick, pierce, stab'), from Proto-Slavic *kolti ('to stab, cleave'), from Proto-Indo-European *kelH- ('to strike, prick').

history.meaning: to stick in, inject (with a needle)

вкусненький.etymology: Affectionate diminutive adjective formed with the suffix -еньк- from вкусный ('tasty, delicious'), derived from вкус ('taste'), from Old Church Slavonic въкусъ ('tasting, trial', ultimately a Gothic borrowing from kausjan 'to taste, test').

вкусный.etymology: Formed with the adjectival suffix -ный from вкус ('taste, flavour'), a deverbal noun from вкусить ('to taste, sample, take a bite of'), built on prefix в- + кусить / кусать ('to bite, taste', from Proto-Slavic *kǫsiti, which itself was an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *kausjaną 'to taste, test, choose', cognate with Gothic kausjan and English choose).

вкуснятина.etymology: Colloquial expressive noun formed with the suffix -ятина from вкусный ('tasty, delicious'), itself from вкус ('taste', Old Church Slavonic въкусъ 'tasting, trial').

владелица.etymology: Feminine agent noun formed with the suffix -ица from владелец ('owner, proprietor'), derived from владеть ('to rule, possess'), a Church Slavonicism from *volděti.

владеть.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic владѣти ('to rule, govern, possess'; compare native East Slavic володѣти), from Proto-Slavic *volděti ('to rule'), cognate with Gothic waldan and English wield.

власть.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic власть ('rule, dominion, authority, power'), corresponding to native East Slavic волость ('district, territory under a ruler', with pleophony -оло-), from Proto-Slavic *volstь, formed with the suffix *-tь from *volsti (1st sg. *voldǫ, 'to rule, govern', whence владеть; cognate with Gothic waldan and English wield).

влезть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from в- ('in, into') + лезть ('to climb, crawl'), from Proto-Slavic *lězti ('to crawl, climb').

history.meaning: to climb in, fit into, intrude

вливаться.etymology: Reflexive and middle-voice form of вливать ('to pour in'), formed from в- ('in, into') + ливать (iterative of лить 'to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to flow into, blend into a group

влиятельный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -тельный from влиять ('to influence') and влияние ('influence', a semantic calque of French influence).

влиять.etymology: Back-formed in the 19th century from влияние ('influence'), which was coined by N. M. Karamzin from Old Church Slavonic въли˫аниѥ ('pouring in') as a calque of French influence / Medieval Latin influentia (from in- 'into' + fluere 'to flow').

вложенный.etymology: Past passive participle of вложить ('to put in, enclose, invest'), formed from в- ('in, into') + ложить ('to lay, place', Proto-Slavic *ložiti).

влюбиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed with the prefix в- ('into') + любить ('to love', from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti) + -ся. Literally, 'to enter into a state of love, fall in love' (constructed with в + accusative: влюбиться в кого-то).

вляпаться.etymology: Colloquial prefixed reflexive verb from в- ('into') + ляпать ('to slap, splash, blunder', an expressive/onomatopoeic Slavic verb *lępati) + -ся, literally 'to step or splash right into mud'.

history.meaning: to step into a mess, land in trouble

вместе.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase въ мѣстѣ ('in [one] place'), combining the preposition въ ('in') with мѣстѣ, the locative singular of мѣсто ('place, spot', modern Russian место): literally 'in the same place', hence 'together'.

вмешать.etymology: Formed with the prefix в- ('in, into') + мешать ('to mix, stir, blend', inherited from Old East Slavic мѣшати and Proto-Slavic *měšati, from Proto-Indo-European *meyḱ- 'to mix', cognate with Latin miscēre and English mix).

history.meaning: to fold in, mix into a batter or dough

вначале.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в начале ('in the beginning'), from в ('in') + locative singular of начало ('beginning', from начать 'to begin', Proto-Slavic *načęlo).

внедриться.etymology: Reflexive form of внедрить ('to implant, introduce, instil'), derived from Old Church Slavonic вънѣдрити ('to place into the bosom/depths'), from въ ('in') + нѣдра ('bosom, depths, interior', Proto-Slavic *nědro).

внеплановый.etymology: 20th-century compound adjective formed from the preposition вне ('outside of', Proto-Slavic *vъně) + плановый ('planned, scheduled', from план 'plan', borrowed via German Plan / French plan from Latin planum).

внешний.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic вънѣшьнии ('outer, external'), formed from the adverb/preposition вънѣ (modern вне 'outside, without', from Proto-Slavic *vъně, related to вон 'out').

внештатный.etymology: Compound administrative adjective formed from вне ('outside of') + штатный ('on the permanent staff/roster'), from штат ('staff establishment, state'), borrowed via German Staat / Dutch staat from Latin status.

вниз.etymology: Formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase в низ ('into the bottom, downward'), combining the directional preposition в ('into') with the accusative of низ ('bottom, lower part', from Proto-Slavic *nizъ).
вниз.notes: Indicates motion downward (*идти вниз* 'go downstairs'); static location below is **внизу**.

внизу.etymology: Formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase в низу ('at the bottom, in the lower part'), combining the preposition в ('in') with the locative singular (-у) of низ ('bottom, lower part', from Proto-Slavic *nizъ).

внимание.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вънимание ('heeding, listening closely, attention'), the verbal noun of вънимати / внимать ('to take in with the mind or ears, heed'), formed from вън- ('into', with epenthetic -н-) and имати ('to take', iterative of яти, Proto-Slavic *jьmati).

внимательно.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of внимательный ('attentive, observant'), derived from внимать ('to heed, listen closely, take in'), built on prefix в- ('in') + -нимать (from Proto-Slavic *jьmati / *jęti 'to take').

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

внимательность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from внимательный ('attentive, observant'), derived from внимать ('to pay heed, take in', from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic вънимати).

вновь.etymology: Univerbation of the Old Russian prepositional phrase въ новь ('into the new, anew'), from въ ('in, into') + новь ('new state, virgin soil', feminine i-stem noun from новый 'new', Proto-Slavic *novь).

внутри.etymology: Univerbation of Old East Slavic вънутри ('on the inside'), combining the preposition въ ('in') + нутри (locative singular of нутро 'interior, insides', from Proto-Slavic *jьnǫtrь / *vъnǫtrь, continuing PIE *h₁en-tero- 'inner', cognate with Latin inter and interior).

внутрь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вънутрь ('into the interior, inward'), combining the directional preposition въ ('into') with the accusative of *nǫtrь ('interior, inside', from Proto-Slavic *vъnǫtrь, PIE *h₁en-tero- 'inner').
внутрь.notes: Indicates inward motion (*проходите внутрь* 'come on inside'), whereas **внутри** indicates static location (*внутри тепло* 'it is warm inside').

внучок.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with the suffix -ок from внук ('grandson'), inherited from Old East Slavic вънукъ ('grandson, descendant'), from Proto-Slavic *vъnukъ (with prosthetic v- before PIE *h₂enōpōts / *nepot-).

внушить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вънушити ('to give ear to; to instil into someone's ears/mind'), formed from вън- ('into') + ухо / уши ('ear / ears', Proto-Slavic *uxo).

history.meaning: to put into the ears, inspire

внятно.etymology: Adverb derived from внятный ('distinct, intelligible, audible'), originally derived from Old Russian въняти ('to attend to, hear, grasp', from вън- + яти 'to take', Proto-Slavic *vъnęti).

вовсе.etymology: Univerbated adverbial phrase formed from the preposition во ('in, into') and все / всё ('all, everything', from Proto-Slavic *vьxъ / *vьśь). Originally meaning 'in all respects, completely, altogether', in modern Russian it is most often used as an intensifier with negation: **вовсе не** / **вовсе нет** ('not at all, by no means').

вода.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вода, from Proto-Slavic *voda, continuing the ancient Proto-Indo-European root *wódr̥ ('water'), cognate with English water, German Wasser, Ancient Greek ὕδωρ, and Lithuanian vanduo.

водить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic водити ('to lead, guide'), from Proto-Slavic *voditi, the iterative-causative counterpart of *vesti ('to lead'), from Proto-Indo-European *wedh- ('to lead').

history.meaning: to lead; to drive a vehicle

водичка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed via водица + -ка from вода ('water'), inherited from Old East Slavic вода, from Proto-Slavic *voda, from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ ('water').

водка.etymology: Formed as a diminutive of вода ('water', Old East Slavic вода, Proto-Slavic *voda) with the suffix -ка. First documented in Russian and Polish sources in the 15th–16th centuries for medicinal herbal tinctures and distilled spirits, paralleling Latin aqua vītae ('water of life') and Gaelic uisge beatha ('whisky').

history.meaning: little water → medicinal tincture, distilled grain spirit

водопад.etymology: Compound noun formed from вода ('water') + connecting vowel -о- + пад- (stem of падать / пасть 'to fall'), calquing German Wasserfall ('waterfall').

военный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from война ('war', Old East Slavic воина), from Proto-Slavic *vojьna ('war, military campaign'), related to *vojь ('warrior').

возбуждающий.etymology: Adjectival present active participle of возбуждать ('to excite, stimulate, arouse'), an Old Church Slavonicism (възбуждати) from въз- ('up') + будити ('to wake, rouse', Proto-Slavic *buditi).

возбуждение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възбуждениѥ ('awakening, stirring up, arousal'), verbal noun of възбудити / възбуждати (from въз- 'up' + будити 'to awaken').

history.meaning: excitement, arousal; initiation (of a legal case)

возбуждённый.etymology: Past passive participle of возбудить ('to excite, rouse, initiate'), from Old Church Slavonic възбудити ('to awaken, rouse'), from въз- + будити ('to wake', Proto-Slavic *buditi).

возвращаться.etymology: Borrowed or reshaped with Church Slavonic vocalism (-вращ- rather than native East Slavic -вороч-) from възвращатися ('to turn back, return'), built on въз- ('back, up') + вращати ('to turn', from Proto-Slavic *vortiti).

возглавить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed with Church Slavonic воз- ('up, onto') + глава ('head, chief', Old Church Slavonic глава, Proto-Slavic *golva), meaning 'to place oneself at the head of, to lead'.

history.meaning: to head, take the lead of

воздаяние.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възда˫аниѥ ('recompense, retribution, reward'), verbal noun of възда˫ати ('to give back, render'), from въз- ('back, in return') + да˫ати ('to give', Proto-Slavic *dajati).

воздух.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въздухъ ('breath, rising vapour, air'), formed from the prefix въз- ('up', Russian воз-) + духъ ('breath, spirit', from Proto-Slavic *duxъ, related to дышать 'to breathe' and дуть 'to blow').

воздушный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from воздух ('air'), from Old Church Slavonic въздухъ ('air, breath, mist rising upward'), from въз- ('up') + духъ ('breath, spirit', Proto-Slavic *duxъ).

возиться.etymology: Reflexive form of возить ('to transport, carry by vehicle; to move about', iterative of везти, Proto-Slavic *voziti) + -ся, developing the colloquial sense 'to bustle about, potter, fuss over'.

history.meaning: to fuss with, potter about, horse around

возле.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic възлѣ ('beside, alongside'), univerbated from the preposition въз ('up along, by') + the locative/dative form лѣ (from the archaic Proto-Slavic root *lě- / *lěv- or *lьg-; Vasmer favors a formation parallel to подлѣ 'beside', remodelled on въз-).

возместить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възмѣстити ('to put in place of, repay, compensate'), from въз- ('in return') + мѣсто ('place', Proto-Slavic *město).

возможно.etymology: Adverb and predicative formed from возможный ('possible'), derived from Old Russian / Church Slavonic възмочь ('to be able, manage'), from въз- + мочь ('to be able, have power', Proto-Slavic *mogti).

возмутительно.etymology: Adverb and predicative derived from возмутительный ('outrageous, indignant'), from возмутить ('to stir up, agitate, shock'), from Church Slavonic възмутити (въз- 'up' + мутити 'to muddy, stir up, trouble', Proto-Slavic *mǫtiti).

вознаграждаться.etymology: Passive and reflexive form of вознаграждать ('to reward, recompense'), formed from воз- ('in return') + награждать ('to reward', from награда 'reward').

возникнуть.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възникнути ('to spring up, rise up, emerge'), formed from въз- ('upward') + никнути ('to sprout, bend or rise', Proto-Slavic *niknǫti).

возобновить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from Church Slavonic воз- ('again, anew') + обновить ('to renew, restore', from об- + новый 'new', Proto-Slavic *novъ).

возражение.etymology: Verbal noun from возразить ('to object, reply against'), formed from Church Slavonic въз- ('back, against') + разити ('to strike', Proto-Slavic *raziti).

возразить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възразити ('to strike back, counter, reply'), formed from въз- ('back, against') + разити ('to strike, hit', Proto-Slavic *raziti), shifting from physical counter-striking to verbal objection.

возродиться.etymology: Reflexive form of возродить ('to regenerate, revive'), from Old Church Slavonic възродити ('to beget anew, regenerate'), from въз- ('anew, up') + родити ('to give birth', Proto-Slavic *roditi).

возрождаться.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of возродиться, formed from Old Church Slavonic възраждати сѧ / Russian возрождать ('to revive, regenerate', from воз- + рождать) + -ся.

воин.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воинъ and Old Church Slavonic воинъ ('warrior, soldier'), formed with the singulative suffix -инъ from вои ('warriors, army'), from Proto-Slavic *vojь ('warrior', PIE *weyh₁- 'to pursue').

война.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воина ('war, military campaign'), from Proto-Slavic *vojьna, derived from *vojь ('warrior; army, host', preserved in воин 'warrior' and войско 'army'), from Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁- ('to pursue, hunt, strive after'; compare Lithuanian výti 'to chase' and Latin vis 'force').

вокзал.etymology: Borrowed in 1837 from English Vauxhall (Vauxhall Gardens, a famous London pleasure garden with a concert pavilion, itself named after the Anglo-Norman lord Falkes de Breauté's hall, Falkes' Hall). When Russia's first railway opened from St Petersburg to Pavlovsk in 1837, the grand musical pavilion at the Pavlovsk terminus was named Вокзал, and the word soon generalized to any major railway station.

history.meaning: London pleasure garden and concert hall

вокзальный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from вокзал ('railway station terminal'), which entered Russian in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries from English Vauxhall (Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens in London), first meaning a concert pavilion at the Pavlovsk terminus of Russia's first railway (1837) and then any major railway station.

history.meaning: railway station → station (adjective: вокзальные часы 'station clock')

волнение.etymology: Verbal noun in -ние formed from волновать / волноваться ('to stir up waves; to agitate, worry'), derived from волна ('wave', from Proto-Slavic *vълna). Preserves both the literal sense 'rough water, choppiness of the sea' and the emotional sense 'nervousness, excitement, agitation'.

history.meaning: surging of waves → agitation, nervousness, excitement

волноваться.etymology: Reflexive form of волновать ('to agitate, stir up waves'), derived from волна ('wave', from Old East Slavic вълна, Proto-Slavic *vълna, from PIE *welH- 'to roll, surge'; cognate with German Welle 'wave'). Literally 'to surge with waves', hence figuratively 'to feel anxious, worry, be nervous'.

history.meaning: wave → to be agitated, worry, be nervous

волос.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic волосъ (showing East Slavic pleophony -оло-; compare Old Church Slavonic власъ and Polish włos), from Proto-Slavic *volsъ ('hair'), with close Indo-Iranian cognates (Avestan varəsa- 'hair of the head', Persian gurs).
волос.notes: Singular **волос** refers to a single strand of hair; hair on the head collectively is plural **волосы** (genitive plural **волос**).

волшебство.etymology: Derived with the abstract suffix -ство from волшебный ('magical') and Old Russian вълшьба ('sorcery, divination'), derived from вълхвъ (волхв, 'pagan magus, sorcerer', Proto-Slavic *vъlxvъ).

вонять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воняти ('to smell, emit an odor', originally either pleasant or unpleasant, as in Church Slavonic благовоние 'fragrance'), denominative from воня (вонь, 'smell, stench'), from Proto-Slavic *vonja (related to *vějati 'to blow').
