порошок.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of порох ('dust, powder; gunpowder'), inherited from Old East Slavic порохъ ('dust, ash'), East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *porxъ ('dust, fine particles'; compare Old Church Slavonic прахъ).

портрет.etymology: Borrowed via German Porträt from French portrait ('likeness, portrait'), originally the past participle of Old French portraire 'to draw forth, depict', from Latin protrahere ('to draw out, bring to light').

порыв.etymology: Deverbal noun from порывать / порвать ('to tear, burst forth'), formed from prefix по- + the root рыв- (lengthened iterative grade of рвать 'to tear, pluck, lunge', from Proto-Slavic *rъvati / *ryvati). Denotes a sudden burst — whether a 'gust' of wind or an emotional 'impulse'.

порядок.etymology: Formed in East Slavic (compare Polish porządek) from по ряду ('in a row, in proper sequence', built on ряд 'row, order', from Proto-Slavic *rędъ) + suffix -ок: 'proper sequence, tidy arrangement, order'.

history.meaning: arrangement in a row → order, proper state

порядок.notes: Takes the locative in **-е**: **всё в порядке** ('everything is in order / all right').

порядочность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость from порядочный ('orderly, decent, honorable'), derived from порядок ('order, sequence'), from по- + ряд ('row, order', Proto-Slavic *rędъ).

посадить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic посадити, formed from the perfective prefix по- and садить ('to make sit, seat, plant'), the Proto-Slavic causative *saditi ('to cause to sit, set') built on the o-grade of *sěděti / *sěsti ('to sit', PIE *sod-éye-ti, exact cognate with English set).

history.meaning: to seat; to plant; to imprison

rootFamily.gloss: to sit; to be in prison

посидеть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the delimitative prefix по- ('for a while, a bit') and сидеть ('to sit'), inherited from Old East Slavic сидѣти and Proto-Slavic *ěděti / *sěděti (from PIE *sed- 'to sit').

history.meaning: to sit for a while; to spend time together

последний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic послѣдьнии ('following behind, last'), formed from по слѣду ('along the track, following after', built on след 'footprint, track', from Proto-Slavic *slědъ) + adjectival suffix -ний.

history.meaning: coming at the end of the trail, last

последствие.etymology: Derived in Old Church Slavonic / bookish Russian послѣдьствие ('following after, result, consequence') from послѣдь ('afterward'), built on слѣдъ ('track, footprint', Proto-Slavic *slědъ).

послезавтра.etymology: Compound adverb formed from после ('after', from Proto-Slavic *poslě) + завтра ('tomorrow', from *za utra 'in the morning').

послужной.etymology: Adjective formed from послуга / послужить ('service, tenure of service'), derived from служить ('to serve'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *služiti ('to serve', from *sluga 'servant').

послушать.etymology: Formed as the perfective counterpart of слушать ('to listen') with the prefix по-. The base verb comes from Old East Slavic слушати ('to listen, obey'), from Proto-Slavic *slušati, built on the same Indo-European root *ḱlew- ('to hear') as слышать.

посметь.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix по- and сметь ('to dare, venture'), inherited from Old East Slavic съмѣти (and Old Church Slavonic съмѣти), from Proto-Slavic *sъměti ('to dare').

посмеяться.etymology: Delimitative/perfective verb formed with prefix по- from смеяться ('to laugh'), inherited from Old East Slavic смѣятисѧ, from Proto-Slavic *smějati sę ('to laugh').

посмотреть.etymology: Formed in Russian as the perfective counterpart of смотреть ('to look, watch') by adding the bounding prefix по-. The base verb comes from Old East Slavic съмотрити ('to look closely, consider'), originally a prefixed derivative of Proto-Slavic *motriti ('to gaze, observe'; compare Lithuanian matýti 'to see').

посоветоваться.etymology: Perfective reflexive formed with prefix по- and -ся from советовать ('to advise, take counsel'), derived from совет ('counsel, advice'), from Old Church Slavonic съвѣтъ (Proto-Slavic *sъvětъ).

посолить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from солить ('to salt'), derived from соль ('salt'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *solь ('salt').

пост.etymology: In the sense 'station, guard post, office', borrowed via French poste or German Posten from Italian posto ('station, place'), from Vulgar Latin *positum (from Latin pōnere 'to place'). (Distinct from religious пост 'fast', an early Germanic loan.)

поставлять.etymology: Imperfective of поставить ('to place, set up; to supply, deliver'), formed with prefix по- from ставить ('to set, place'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *staviti.

поставщик.etymology: Agent noun formed with suffix -щик from поставка / поставлять ('to supply, deliver'), derived from по- + ставить ('to set, place, furnish', Proto-Slavic *staviti).

постановить.etymology: Formed with prefix по- from становить ('to set up, establish, decide'), derived from стан ('stand, camp, frame') / стать ('to stand'), from Proto-Slavic *stanoviti.

постельный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from постель ('bed, bedding'), inherited from Old East Slavic постеля ('bedding, spread'), derived from по- + стлать (стелю, 'to spread, lay out'), from Proto-Slavic *postelja.

посторожить.etymology: Formed with the delimitative/perfective prefix по- ('for a while') + сторожить ('to guard, watch over'), derived from сторож ('watchman, guard', from Proto-Slavic *storgъ with East Slavic pleophony -оро-).

history.meaning: to guard, keep watch over for a while

посторонний.etymology: Adjective formed from по стороне ('off to the side, outside'), derived from сторона ('side, region'), East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *storna ('side, direction').

постоянно.etymology: Adverb formed from постоянный ('constant, permanent, steady'), derived from постоять ('to stand firm, abide'), built from по- + стоять ('to stand', from Proto-Slavic *stojati; compare Latin cōnstāns 'standing firm, constant').

постоять.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the delimitative prefix по- ('for a while') and стоять ('to stand'), inherited from Old East Slavic постояти, from Proto-Slavic *postojati (from PIE *stā- / *steh₂- 'to stand'). With за + accusative (постоять за себя), it means 'to stand up for, defend'.

history.meaning: to stand for a while; to defend
to stand for a while; to stand up for

пострадать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from страдать ('to suffer, endure hardship'), inherited from Old East Slavic страдати ('to labor hard, suffer'), from Proto-Slavic *stradati.

постричь.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from стричь ('to shear, cut hair'), inherited from Old East Slavic стричи (стригу), from Proto-Slavic *strigti ('to shear, clip').

построить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix по- and строить ('to build, construct; to arrange'), inherited from Old East Slavic строити ('to arrange, order, prepare, build'), from Proto-Slavic *strojiti, causative/denominative from *strojь ('order, arrangement, structure').

постройка.etymology: Noun in -ка formed from построить ('to build, construct'), derived with prefix по- from строить ('to arrange, build'), from строй ('order, array'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *strojiti.

поступить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поступити ('to step forward, proceed, act'), formed from the prefix по- and ступить ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti). From 'stepping forward', it developed both the sense 'to act, behave' (поступить правильно) and 'to enter, enroll in an institution' (поступить в университет).

history.meaning: to act, behave; to enroll, enter

rootFamily.gloss: to step on; to arrive (of time)

постучать.etymology: Formed with the perfective/delimitative prefix по- ('a little, for a moment') + стучать ('to knock, tap, rap'), built on the Slavic sound-symbolic root *stuk- ('knock, thud').

посчитать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from считать ('to count, consider'), inherited from Old East Slavic съчитати ('to read/count together'), from Proto-Slavic *sъ-čitati.

посылать.etymology: Imperfective of послать ('to send'), formed with prefix по- and lengthened-grade iterative stem -сылать from слать (шлю, 'to send'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъlati.

потерянный.etymology: Past passive participle of потерять ('to lose'), formed with perfective prefix по- + терять ('to lose, waste, shed', from Old East Slavic теряти, related to тереть 'to rub away, wear down').

потихонечку.etymology: Affectionate/diminutive adverb formed with prefix по- and double diminutive suffix -оньк-/-ечк- from тихо ('quietly, slowly'), from тихий ('quiet, still', Proto-Slavic *tixъ).

потише.etymology: Attenuative comparative formed with prefix по- ('a little') from тише ('quieter'), comparative of тихий ('quiet, soft'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *tixъ.

поток.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic потокъ ('stream, torrent'), formed from по- + ток ('flow, current'), o-grade noun from течь ('to flow, run', Proto-Slavic *tokъ / *tekti).

потом.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase по томь ('after that'), combining the preposition по ('after') with томь, the locative singular of the demonstrative pronoun то ('that', from Proto-Slavic *to).

потому.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase по тому ('by that, on account of that'), combining the preposition по ('along, by, because of') with тому, the dative singular of то ('that'). Most frequently used in the compound conjunction потому что ('because', literally 'on account of that which').

history.meaning: by that, on account of that

потратить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from тратить ('to spend, expend, waste'), inherited from Old East Slavic тратити ('to consume, destroy, spend'), from Proto-Slavic *tratiti.

history.meaning: to spend, to waste, to use up

потревожить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from тревожить ('to disturb, alarm'), derived from тревога ('alarm, anxiety, commotion'), likely connected with отвага or older тривога.

потрудиться.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from трудиться ('to labor, take pains'), derived from труд ('labor, toil, effort'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *trudъ ('toil, hardship').

history.meaning: to take the trouble, to bother

поужинать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from ужинать ('to have supper/dinner'), derived from ужин ('evening meal', originally 'midday/south meal'), from Old East Slavic ужинъ, derived from югъ / угъ ('south, midday sun', Proto-Slavic *jugъ).

поучиться.etymology: Delimitative/perfective verb formed with prefix по- from учиться ('to learn, study'), reflexive of учить ('to teach'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *učiti.

похвастаться.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from хвастаться ('to boast, brag'), derived from хвастать, from Proto-Slavic *xvastati ('to babble, brag', of expressive/onomatopoeic origin).

похоже.etymology: Neuter short form and adverb of похожий ('similar, resembling'), derived from походить ('to take after, resemble', from по- + ходить 'to walk, go'). Used both as a predicate ('it looks like, it is similar') and as a parenthetical discourse marker ('it seems, apparently').

history.meaning: similar → alike; it seems, looks like

похожий.etymology: Derived from походить ('to resemble, take after, go along someone's path'), built from the prefix по- ('along, after') and ходить ('to walk, go', Proto-Slavic *xoditi), with the alternation д > ж before the adjectival suffix -ий. Literally, 'walking in the same way, taking after'.

history.meaning: taking after in gait/manner → similar, resembling

поцеловать.etymology: Perfective counterpart of целовать ('to kiss'), formed with the prefix по- from Old East Slavic цѣловати ('to greet, wish good health; to kiss'), derived from цѣлъ / целый ('whole, hale, healthy', Proto-Slavic *cělъ).

history.meaning: whole, hale → to wish health in greeting, kiss

поцелуй.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from the imperative stem of поцеловать ('to kiss'), from по- + целовать ('to kiss, greet', originally 'to wish someone whole/healthy'), derived from целый ('whole, intact', Proto-Slavic *cělъ).

почему.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase по чему ('along/by what?, on account of what?'), combining the preposition по with чему, the dative singular of что ('what', from Old East Slavic чьто).

почесать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from чесать ('to scratch, comb'), inherited from Old East Slavic чесати, from Proto-Slavic *česati ('to comb, scratch, strip').

почитать.etymology: Delimitative perfective formed with prefix по- ('for a while, a little') from читать ('to read'), inherited from Old East Slavic читати, iterative of чьсти ('to read, count, honor', Proto-Slavic *čitati).

почка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пъчька / почка ('bud, swelling; kidney'), diminutive of archaic *пъка ('swelling, bulge'), from Proto-Slavic *pъkati ('to swell, burst open, bud').

почтение.etymology: Verbal noun from почтить ('to honor, respect'), inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic почьтение ('respect, reverence'), from по- + чьсти ('to honor, revere', Proto-Slavic *čьsti).

почём.etymology: Adverbialized prepositional phrase formed from по ('at the rate of, for') + чём (locative singular of что 'what', from Proto-Slavic *čьto), literally 'at what price each?'.

history.meaning: for how much, at what price

пошутить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from шутить ('to joke, jest'), derived from шут ('jester, fool'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *šutъ.

history.meaning: to joke, to make a joke

поэзия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish poezja or German Poesie from Latin poēsis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis, 'making, creation, poetry'), from ποιέω (poiéō, 'to make, compose').

поэт.etymology: Borrowed via French poète or German Poet from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, 'maker, creator, poet'), agent noun from ποιέω ('to make, compose').

появиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed with the prefix по- from явиться ('to appear, show oneself'), derived from явить ('to show, manifest'), from Old East Slavic явити and Proto-Slavic *javiti ('to make visible, reveal', from *javъ 'awake, manifest, open', as in наяву 'in waking life', cognate with Sanskrit āvíṣ 'openly, before the eyes').

history.meaning: manifest, visible → to show oneself, appear

правда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic правьда ('truth, justice, law code' — famously in Русская правда, the 11th-century Kievan legal code), from Proto-Slavic *pravьda, formed from *pravъ ('straight, right, just, true') + the abstract suffix *-ьda.

rootFamily.gloss: to tuck in, make a bed

правее.etymology: Comparative form in -ее of правый ('right, on the right-hand side'), inherited from Old East Slavic правыи ('straight, right, just'), from Proto-Slavic *pravъ.

правильно.etymology: Adverb formed from правильный ('correct, right, proper'), derived from правило ('rule, straightedge, rudder'), itself built with the instrument suffix -ло on правый ('straight, right, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

правильный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from правило ('rule, straightedge, guide'), derived from правый ('straight, right, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ). Literally, 'conforming to the rule or straight line'.

правитель.etymology: Agent noun in -тель formed from править ('to rule, govern, steer, direct'), derived from правый ('straight, right'), from Proto-Slavic *praviti ('to make straight, guide, rule').

право.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic право ('right, justice, law'), substantivized neuter singular of правыи / правый ('straight, right, just, true'), from Proto-Slavic *pravъ ('straight, right'). Parallels the semantic development of German Recht and French droit ('straight → right, law').

праздник.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic праздьникъ 'feast day, holiday', derived from праздьнъ ('unoccupied, free from everyday labour', from Proto-Slavic *porzdьnъ): a day set free from ordinary work for celebration.
праздник.notes: The middle consonant -д- is silent in everyday pronunciation (pronounced [празник], spelled праздник).

праздничный.etymology: Relational and qualitative adjective formed with the suffix -ный from праздник ('holiday, celebration', with к → ч before -н-), adopted from Old Church Slavonic праздьникъ ('feast day', from праздьнъ 'unoccupied, free from work').
праздничный.notes: Like *праздник*, the middle -д- is silent in standard speech: pronounced [пра́зничный].

практически.etymology: Adverb formed from практический ('practical'), borrowed via German praktisch / French pratique from Late Latin practicus, from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós, 'fit for action, practical', from πράσσω 'to do, act').

прачечная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from прачечный, derived from прачка ('laundress, washerwoman'), diminutive of archaic прачька / праля, from Proto-Slavic *pьrati ('to beat laundry with a wash-beetle, wash clothes').

превращаться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form in -ся of превращать ('to transform, turn into'), adopted with Church Slavonic vocalism (пре- 'across, over' + вращать 'to turn', corresponding to native East Slavic пере- + ворочать, from Proto-Slavic *vortiti).

history.meaning: to transform → to turn into, be transformed into

предавать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдавати (imperfective of прѣдати 'to hand over, deliver up, betray', with non-pleophonic прѣ- < *per-), from Proto-Slavic *per-dati ('to give over').

history.meaning: to hand over, deliver up, betray
to betray, to be unfaithful to

предатель.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдатель ('betrayer, traitor, Judas'), formed with the agent suffix -тель from прѣдати / предать ('to hand over, deliver up to an enemy, betray'), a compound of прѣ- ('over, across') + дати ('to give', Russian дать; compare Latin trāditor 'traitor' from trāns-dare 'to hand over').

предлагать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдълагати ('to lay before, set forth, offer'), formed from the Church Slavonic prefix прѣдъ- ('before, in front of', East Slavic перед-) and -лагати (iterative of ложити 'to lay, place'). Literally, 'to lay something before someone' (an exact structural parallel to Latin prōpōnere 'to propose').

предложение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъложение ('setting forth, presentation, offering'), the verbal noun of прѣдъложити / предложить ('to lay before, offer, propose'). In the 18th century, Russian grammarians (such as Lomonosov) also used it to calque Latin prōpositiō ('grammatical clause/sentence, logical proposition').

предполагаемый.etymology: Present passive participle of предполагать ('to suppose, presume, assume'), formed with Old Church Slavonic prefix пред- ('before, fore-') + полагать ('to lay, suppose', from Proto-Slavic *polagati), calquing Latin suppōnere / German voraussetzen.

предприниматель.etymology: Calque on French entrepreneur or German Unternehmer, formed from предпринимать ('to undertake', from пред- 'before' + принимать 'to take') + agent suffix -тель.

history.meaning: one who undertakes a business venture

предсказание.etymology: Verbal noun in -ание from предсказать ('to foretell, predict'), modelled with the Church Slavonic prefix пред- ('before, in advance', calquing Latin prae-dicere) + сказать ('to say, tell', from Proto-Slavic *sъkazati).

предстоять.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъстояти ('to stand before, be imminent'), formed from прѣдъ- ('before, in front of') + стояти ('to stand', Proto-Slavic *stojati).

history.meaning: to lie ahead, be in store

предупредить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдоупрѣдити ('to go ahead of, forestall, anticipate'), formed from прѣдъ- ('before') + оу- + прѣдити ('to go in front', from предъ / перед 'in front', Proto-Slavic *perdъ). In the 18th century, influenced by French prévenir ('to go before → to forewarn, notify in advance'), it acquired the modern meaning 'to warn'.

history.meaning: to forestall → to warn, notify in advance

предупреждать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of предупредить ('to warn, notify in advance; to prevent'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдоупрѣждати (showing the Church Slavonic reflex -жд- for Proto-Slavic *dj), built on предъ / перед ('before, in front').

history.meaning: to warn, notify in advance; to forestall

предупреждающий.etymology: Present active participle of предупреждать ('to warn, forestall'), borrowed with Church Slavonic vocalism (пред- 'before, in advance' + у- + преждать 'to go ahead of, anticipate', from передить / перед 'front', Proto-Slavic *perdъ).

предчувствие.etymology: Formed as a calque on French pressentiment or German Vorgefühl from пред- ('before, fore-') + чувствие / чувство ('feeling, sense', from Proto-Slavic *čuvьstvo, from *čuti 'to feel, perceive').

прежний.etymology: Adjective formed from прежде ('before, formerly'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣжде (with жд < *dj; compare native East Slavic переже), comparative of *perdъ ('front, before').

history.meaning: former, previous, the same as before

президент.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century, initially for heads of state colleges and academies, later for heads of republic states) via German Präsident and French président from Latin praesidēns (genitive praesidentis, 'presiding officer, governor'), present participle of praesidēre ('to sit before, preside over, guard', from prae- 'before' + sedēre 'to sit').

history.meaning: to sit in front / preside → presiding head

прекратить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣкратити ('to cut short, abridge, terminate'), formed from the prefix прѣ- (East Slavic пере-) and кратити ('to shorten', from кратъкъ 'short', East Slavic короткий, from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ). Literally, прекратить means 'to cut short'.

history.meaning: to cut short, bring to an end

преподавать.etymology: Imperfective of преподать ('to impart, give, teach'), formed with Old Church Slavonic prefix пре- + по- + давать ('to give', Proto-Slavic *davati), developing the specialized sense 'to lecture, teach a subject'.

history.meaning: to teach (at a school or university)

прервать.etymology: Formed with Old Church Slavonic prefix пре- ('across, through', corresponding to native пере-) from рвать ('to tear, break'), from Proto-Slavic *rъvati.

пресечение.etymology: Verbal noun from пресечь ('to cut across, cut off, put a stop to'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣсѣчение, from прѣ- ('across') + сѣщи ('to cut, hew', Proto-Slavic *sěkti).

преступник.etymology: Agent noun in -ник derived from преступить ('to step across, transgress, violate the law'), formed with Old Church Slavonic prefix пре- ('across, over') + ступить ('to step', Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti).

прибыть.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('to, arrival, addition') from быть ('to be'), inherited from Old East Slavic прибыти, from Proto-Slavic *pri-byti.

history.meaning: to come to be at a place, arrive, increase

привал.etymology: Deverbal noun from привалить ('to roll/lean against, moor a boat to shore, halt on a march to rest'), formed from при- ('to, against') + валить ('to roll, lean, throng', Proto-Slavic *valiti).

привет.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic привѣтъ ('friendly welcome, greeting, affable speech'), a deverbal noun from привѣтити ('to greet, welcome warmly'), built from prefix при- + *větъ ('speech, counsel, address', the same Proto-Slavic root seen in ответ 'answer' and совет 'advice'). In the 20th century Привет! became the standard informal greeting 'Hi! / Hello!'.

привлечь.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic привлѣщи ('to draw toward, attract', compare native East Slavic приволочь), from Proto-Slavic *pri-velkti ('to drag/draw toward').

привычка.etymology: Noun in -ка derived from привыкнуть ('to get used to, become accustomed'), formed with prefix при- from выкнуть ('to learn by habit, grow accustomed'), from Proto-Slavic *vyknǫti (related to учить and навык).

приглядеть.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('attentively, watching over') from глядеть ('to look'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *ględěti ('to look, gaze').

history.meaning: to look after, to keep an eye on

приглядеться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of приглядеть, formed from при- ('closely, accustomed to') + глядеть ('to look', Proto-Slavic *ględěti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to take a closer look, to observe closely

приготовить.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix при- + готовить ('to prepare, make ready; to cook'), derived from готовый ('ready', from Old East Slavic готовыи and Proto-Slavic *gotovъ).

history.meaning: to prepare, make ready; to cook (a dish or meal)

придумать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix при- (indicating addition or mental attainment) and думать ('to think'), from Old East Slavic думати and Proto-Slavic *dumati (from *duma 'thought, counsel', an early borrowing from Gothic dōms 'judgment').

приезжать.etymology: Imperfective partner of приехать ('to arrive by vehicle'), formed from the arrival prefix при- + езжать (iterative stem of ездить / ехать 'to travel by vehicle, ride', from Proto-Slavic *ěxati / *ězditi).

morphemes.meaning: ride, travel by vehicle (ездить, with зд → зж)

признавать.etymology: Imperfective of признать ('to recognize, acknowledge, confess'), formed with prefix при- from знать ('to know'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *znati.

признание.etymology: Verbal noun in -ние from признать ('to acknowledge, confess, recognize'), formed from при- + знать ('to know', Proto-Slavic *znati).

признательный.etymology: Adjective in -тельный formed from признавать / признать ('to acknowledge [a debt or kindness]'), calquing French reconnaissant ('grateful', literally 'recognizing'), built on знать ('to know').

признаться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from признать ('to recognize, acknowledge'), built from the prefix при- and знать ('to know', from Proto-Slavic *znati, PIE *ǵneh₃-). With the reflexive suffix -ся, признаться means 'to acknowledge about oneself, confess, admit' (often in love: признаться в любви).

прийти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic приити / прити ('to come, arrive on foot'), formed from the prefix при- ('up to, arrival') + идти ('to walk, go', Old East Slavic ити, from Proto-Slavic *iti). Like идти, it takes its past tense (пришёл, пришла, пришли) from the suppletive stem *šьd-.

прийтись.etymology: Perfective reflexive/impersonal verb formed by adding -сь to прийти ('to come, arrive on foot', from при- + идти, Proto-Slavic *prijьti). From the concrete sense of two parts 'coming together into alignment, fitting' (прийтись по вкусу 'to suit one's taste'), the impersonal dative construction мне пришлось + infinitive developed the sense 'it fell to my lot to, I had to'.

history.meaning: to come to fit, fall to someone's lot
to fit; (impersonal + dat.) to have to

rootFamily.gloss: to have to (impf.); to be related to

приказать.etymology: Formed with prefix при- from казать ('to show, say, order'), inherited from Old East Slavic приказати ('to order, entrust'), from Proto-Slavic *pri-kazati.

приключение.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from приключиться ('to happen unexpectedly, befall'), built on prefix при- + ключиться ('to happen, fit together like a key or hook', from ключ 'hook, key', Proto-Slavic *kľučь). Originally 'an unexpected event or occurrence', then an 'adventure'.

history.meaning: to happen, befall → unexpected occurrence, adventure

прикольный.etymology: Late 20th-century slang adjective formed with -ный from прикол ('joke, gag, fun thing'), deverbal noun from приколоть / прикалываться ('to pin; in slang, to crack jokes, needle, have fun'), from при- + колоть ('to prick, pin', Proto-Slavic *kolti).

прикончить.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('completely, to the end') from кончить ('to finish, end'), derived from конец ('end'), from Proto-Slavic *konьcь.

history.meaning: to finish off, to kill, to bump off

прикрепить.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('to, onto') from крепить ('to fasten, strengthen'), derived from крепкий ('strong, firm'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *krěpъ ('strong, firm').

history.meaning: to attach, to assign, to fasten

прикрыть.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('slightly; protectively') from крыть ('to cover'), inherited from Old East Slavic крыти, from Proto-Slavic *kryti ('to cover, hide').

прилипчивый.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -чивый from прилипать / прилипнуть ('to stick to, cling to'), from при- ('to') + липнуть ('to stick, adhere', from Proto-Slavic *lьpnǫti / *lipati).

прилично.etymology: Adverb formed from приличный ('decent, proper, seemly'), originally 'fitting the face/person, suitable', from при- + лик / лицо ('face, appearance', Proto-Slavic *likъ).

приличный.etymology: Inherited via Old East Slavic приличьныи ('similar, fitting, seemly'), formed from при- + лик / лицо ('face, form, appearance', Proto-Slavic *likъ), shifting from 'matching in appearance, suitable' to 'decent, respectable, sizable'.

приложение.etymology: Verbal noun from приложить ('to lay beside, attach, apply'), formed from при- ('to, beside') + ложить ('to lay, place', Proto-Slavic *ložiti); the modern computing sense 'app' is a semantic calque of English application.

прилёт.etymology: Deverbal noun from прилететь ('to arrive by flying'), formed from при- ('arrival') + лёт / лететь ('to fly', inherited from Proto-Slavic *letěti).

примерный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from пример ('example, model; approximate measure'), derived from примерить ('to measure against, try on'), from при- + мера ('measure', Proto-Slavic *měra).

принести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic принести ('to bring by carrying'), formed from the arrival prefix при- + нести ('to carry on foot', from Proto-Slavic *nesti, from PIE *h₁neḱ- 'to reach, carry, obtain').

принимать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of принять ('to take, accept, receive'), inherited from Old East Slavic приимати, formed from the prefix при- ('to, towards') and -нимать (with epenthetic н- reanalyzed from prefixes ending in a nasal, from Old East Slavic имати 'to take', iterative of яти, Proto-Slavic *jьmati).

history.meaning: to receive, accept, take (medicine, guests, a shower, or a decision)

принтер.etymology: Late 20th-century borrowing from English printer, agent/instrument noun from print (from Old French preinte 'impression', from Latin premere 'to press').

принцип.etymology: Borrowed via German Prinzip or French principe from Latin principium ('beginning, foundation, fundamental rule'), derived from princeps ('first, chief', from primus 'first' + capere 'to take').

принципиальность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость formed from принципиальный ('principled, of principle'), derived from принцип (from Latin principium 'foundation, principle').

принятие.etymology: Verbal noun from принять ('to take, accept, adopt'), inherited from Old East Slavic приняти, from Proto-Slavic *pri-jęti ('to take to oneself, receive', from *jęti 'to take').

приобщить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приобъщити ('to make a partaker, unite with, add to'), formed from при- + общий ('common, shared', from Proto-Slavic *obьťь).

history.meaning: to join to a whole, associate
to add, to attach (to a case file); to acquaint with

приписать.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('in addition, onto') from писать ('to write'), inherited from Old East Slavic писати, from Proto-Slavic *pisati.

history.meaning: to ascribe, credit, add in writing

приписка.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ка from приписать ('to add in writing, append a note'), built on prefix при- ('in addition, onto') + писать ('to write', from Proto-Slavic *pьsati).

history.meaning: to add in writing → postscript, added written note

припугнуть.etymology: Formed with attenuative prefix при- ('slightly, a little') from пугнуть ('to frighten, startle'), semelfactive of пугать ('to scare').

history.meaning: to scare a little, to give a fright

прирождённый.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прирожденъ (with жд < *dj), past passive participle of природити ('to beget, endow by birth'), from при- + родити ('to give birth', Proto-Slavic *roditi).

присаживаться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective formed with attenuative prefix при- ('for a moment, on the edge') from саживаться / садиться ('to sit down'), from Proto-Slavic *saditi ('to seat').

history.meaning: to take a seat, to sit down

присмотр.etymology: Deverbal noun from присмотреть ('to look after, watch over'), formed with prefix при- ('attentively') from смотреть ('to look, watch', Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti).

приспособленный.etymology: Past passive participle of приспособить ('to adapt, fit'), formed from при- + способ ('way, method, means', borrowed via Polish sposób or formed from пособь 'help, aid', related to поcобить and себе).

приставка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from приставить ('to set against, attach, place beside'), built from при- ('to, beside') + ставить ('to put, set upright', from Proto-Slavic *staviti). In the 18th century Russian grammarians used приставка to calque Latin praefixum ('prefix'); in the late 20th century (from телеприставка / игровая приставка, an electronic unit attached to a TV set), it became the everyday word for a video game console or set-top box.

пристально.etymology: Adverb formed from пристальный ('intent, fixed, steadfast'), derived from пристать ('to stick to, cleave to, fix one's gaze on'), from при- + стать ('to stand', Proto-Slavic *stati).

history.meaning: to stand close to, cleave to

приступ.etymology: Deverbal noun from приступить ('to step up to, assault, attack'), formed from при- ('up to, against') + ступить ('to step, tread', Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti), denoting both a military storming and a sudden fit of illness.

приступать.etymology: Imperfective of приступить ('to step up to, set about, begin'), formed with prefix при- ('up to') from ступать ('to step, tread'), from Proto-Slavic *stǫpati.

причём.etymology: Conjunction lexicalized from the prepositional phrase при чём ('in addition to which, side by side with what'), from при ('at, beside, in the presence of') + чём (locative of что 'what', Proto-Slavic *čьto).

history.meaning: and that, what is more, moreover

пришить.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('onto, attaching') from шить ('to sew'), inherited from Old East Slavic шити, from Proto-Slavic *šiti ('to sew', from Proto-Indo-European *syuh₁-).

history.meaning: to sew on, stitch back on

прищуриться.etymology: Formed with the attenuative prefix при- ('slightly, partly') + щуриться ('to screw up one's eyes, squint'), built on the Slavic root *ščur- ('to narrow the eyes against bright light'; compare пращур and Czech mžourat).

history.meaning: to screw up one's eyes → to squint slightly, narrow one's eyes

приятный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приятьныи ('acceptable, welcome, pleasing'), formed from прияти ('to receive, accept warmly', modern Russian принять, built on *pri- + *jęti 'to take') + suffix -ный: literally 'well-received, welcome, agreeable'.
приятный.notes: Heard every day at meals in **Приятного аппетита!** ('Bon appétit!') and on meeting someone in **Очень приятно!** ('Pleased to meet you!').

приём.etymology: Deverbal noun from принять (Old East Slavic прияти, present прииму, 'to take, receive, grasp'), from Proto-Slavic *pri-jęmъ ('taking, reception, hold', from *jęti 'to take').

приёмчик.etymology: Diminutive in -чик of приём ('fighting hold, trick, technique, reception'), from Proto-Slavic *pri-jęmъ ('taking, grip', from *jęti 'to take, grasp').

проба.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Probe and Polish próba ('test, trial, assay of precious metal') from Medieval Latin proba ('test, proof'), back-formed from Latin probāre ('to test, try, find good', from probus 'good, upright').

history.meaning: trial, test batch, tasting; fineness hallmark

пробить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пробити ('to pierce through, strike'), formed with prefix про- ('through; completing a chime') + бить ('to beat, strike', from Proto-Slavic *biti). Used both for piercing an opening and for a clock striking the hour.

history.meaning: to strike (the hour); to pierce, punch through

проблемный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from проблема ('problem'), borrowed via Polish problema / German Problem from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, 'something thrown forward, obstacle, question for solution', from προβάλλω).

проваливать.etymology: Imperfective of провалить ('to cause to collapse/fall through, ruin, fail'), formed with prefix про- ('through') from валить ('to topple, roll', Proto-Slavic *valiti); in colloquial imperatives (проваливай!), 'to clear off, get lost'.

history.meaning: to fail, to botch; (colloq.) to get lost

провалить.etymology: Formed with prefix про- ('through, down into a hole') from валить ('to tumble, topple'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *valiti ('to roll, fell').

проверить.etymology: Formed in Russian from prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') + верить / вера ('to verify, test against truth / faith, trust', from Proto-Slavic *věra, cognate with Latin vērus 'true' and German wahr): literally 'to test whether something is true'.

history.meaning: to test for truth, check, verify

провинция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish prowincja or German Provinz from Latin prōvincia ('territory outside Italy under a Roman magistrate, province').

проводить.etymology: Formed from the prefix про- ('through, along') and водить ('to lead, conduct', iterative of вести, from Proto-Slavic *voditi). Represents two homographic verbs in Russian: (1) perfective проводить (paired with провожать), meaning 'to escort, see off, accompany to the door or station', and (2) imperfective проводить (paired with провести), meaning 'to conduct, spend (time), or carry out'.

history.meaning: to see off, escort (pf.); to spend time, conduct (impf.)

провокатор.etymology: Borrowed via French provocateur or German Provokateur from Latin prōvocātor ('challenger, instigator'), agent noun from prōvocāre ('to call forth, challenge', from prō- + vocāre 'to call').

провороваться.etymology: Formed with prefix про- (indicating ruin or exposure through an action) and reflexive -ся from воровать ('to steal'), derived from вор ('thief, criminal').

history.meaning: to be caught stealing, embezzle to one's ruin

проголодаться.etymology: Formed with prefix про- ('thoroughly, over time') and -ся from голодать ('to be hungry, starve'), derived from голод ('hunger'), East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *goldъ.

программа.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via French programme or German Programm from Late Latin programma ('public notice, edict'), from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma, 'public written notice, agenda'), from προγράφω (prográphō, 'to write beforehand or in public', from προ- 'before, forth' + γράφω 'to write').

прогрессивный.etymology: Borrowed via French progressif or German progressiv (with Russian suffix -ный), derived from Latin prōgressus ('an advance, going forward', from prōgredī 'to step forward').

прогрессировать.etymology: Borrowed via German progressieren or formed from прогресс ('progress'), ultimately from Latin prōgressus ('going forward', from prō- + gradī 'to step, walk').

прогреться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of прогреть ('to warm through'), formed with prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') from греть ('to warm, heat'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěti.

прогулка.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ка from прогуляться / прогулять ('to take a walk, stroll'), built on the prefix про- + гулять ('to walk, stroll at leisure').

history.meaning: to go for a stroll → a walk, stroll, outing

продаваться.etymology: Passive/intransitive form in -ся of продавать ('to sell'), inherited from Old East Slavic продавати, built on про- + давать ('to give', from Proto-Slavic *prodavati).

history.meaning: to sell → to be sold, be on sale

продаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of продать ('to sell'), inherited from Old East Slavic продати, from Proto-Slavic *pro-dati ('to give away for a price, sell', from *dati 'to give').

history.meaning: to sell oneself, to sell out

проделка.etymology: Noun in -ка formed from проделать ('to carry out, pull off [a trick]'), derived from про- + делать ('to do, make', from Proto-Slavic *dělati).

продолжать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of продолжить ('to lengthen, prolong, continue'), formed from the prefix про- and должить ('to make long'), derived from долгий ('long', Old East Slavic дългыи, Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ, cognate with English long and Latin indulgeo). Literally, 'to draw out in length, prolong'.

продолжаться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form in -ся of продолжать ('to continue, prolong'), derived from продолжить, built on долгий ('long'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *dьlgъ ('long').

продуктовый.etymology: Adjective formed with -овый from продукты ('foodstuffs, groceries'), plural of продукт ('product, produce'), borrowed via German Produkt from Latin prōductum ('something brought forth', from prōdūcere).

history.meaning: that which is produced, brought forth

продумать.etymology: Formed with prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') from думать ('to think'), inherited from Old East Slavic думати ('to take counsel, think'), from Proto-Slavic *dumati (from *duma 'thought, counsel').

history.meaning: to think through, to plan out

продуть.etymology: Formed with prefix про- ('through') from дуть ('to blow'), inherited from Old East Slavic дути (дую), from Proto-Slavic *duti ('to blow').

history.meaning: to blow through; catch a chill/draft; (colloq.) lose a game

проект.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century, often spelled прожект from French before settling on проект after German Projekt) from Latin prōiectum ('something thrown forth, plan, design'), neuter past participle of prōicere ('to throw forward, stretch out', from prō- 'forth' + iacere 'to throw').

прожевать.etymology: Formed with the completive prefix про- ('thoroughly, all the way through') + жевать ('to chew'), inherited from Old East Slavic жевати / жьвати and Proto-Slavic *žьvati ('to chew', directly cognate with English chew and German kauen).

прозвенеть.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix про- + звенеть ('to ring, jingle, clink'), inherited from Old East Slavic звьнѣти and Proto-Slavic *zvьněti, related by ablaut to звон ('ringing, peal') and звук ('sound').

прозвище.etymology: Derived with suffix -ище from прозвать ('to call by a byname, nickname'), formed from про- + звать ('to call, name', inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъvati).

прозрачно.etymology: Adverb formed from прозрачный ('transparent, pellucid, clear'), borrowed with Old Church Slavonic vocalism -зрач- from *prozračьnъ ('looking through'), built on про- ('through') + зракъ ('sight, look', from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti 'to see, look').

проигранный.etymology: Past passive participle of проиграть ('to lose in a game or contest'), formed with prefix про- (indicating loss) from играть ('to play', from Proto-Slavic *jьgrati).

проиграть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix про- (in the sense of loss, forfeiture, or spending through an action) and играть ('to play'), from Old East Slavic играти and Proto-Slavic *jьgrati.

history.meaning: to lose (in a game, bet, or contest)

произведение.etymology: Verbal noun from произвести ('to bring forth, produce, create'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic произведение ('bringing forth, creation'), from про- + из- + вести ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *vesti), calquing Latin prōductiō.

производственный.etymology: Adjective formed from производство ('production, manufacture, industry'), derived from производить ('to produce, bring forth'), from про- + из- + водить ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *voditi).

произойти.etymology: Perfective counterpart of происходить ('to happen, occur; to originate from'), formed from про- ('forth, through') + из- / изо- ('out of') + йти / идти ('to go', Proto-Slavic *iti). Literally, 'to come forth out of', whence 'to come to pass, happen, occur'.

history.meaning: to come forth, issue → to happen, take place

проинспектировать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix про- from инспектировать ('to inspect'), borrowed via German inspizieren from Latin īnspectāre / īnspicere, īnspectum ('to look into, examine').

происходить.etymology: Imperfective verb borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic происходити ('to go forth, issue from, originate'), formed from про- ('forth, through') + ис- / из- ('out of') + ходити ('to go, walk'). From 'coming forth, originating', it developed the modern meaning 'to happen, take place'.

history.meaning: to happen, occur; to originate from

проклясть.etymology: Formed with prefix про- from клясть (кляну, 'to curse, swear'), inherited from Old East Slavic прокляти, from Proto-Slavic *pro-klęti ('to curse, execrate', from *klęti 'to swear, curse').

пролежать.etymology: Formed with the perdurative prefix про- ('through a whole span of time') + лежать ('to lie', inherited from Old East Slavic лежати and Proto-Slavic *ležati).

history.meaning: to lie (somewhere for a specified period of time)

промах.etymology: Deverbal noun from промахнуть / промахнуться ('to swing past the mark, miss'), formed from про- ('past, by') + махать / махнуть ('to wave, swing', inherited from Proto-Slavic *maxati).

пронзить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проньзити ('to pierce through, stab'), formed with prefix про- ('through') from ньзити / нъзити ('to pierce, thrust in', Proto-Slavic *nьziti, with Proto-Slavic third palatalization *g > *z from the root of нож 'knife' and заноза 'splinter').

пропавший.etymology: Past active participle of пропасть ('to fall through, disappear, be lost'), formed with prefix про- ('through, away') from пасть ('to fall', inherited from Proto-Slavic *pasti).

пропустить.etymology: Formed with the prefix про- ('through, past') + пустить ('to let go, allow to pass', from Old East Slavic пустити and Proto-Slavic *pustiti). Depending on context, 'letting something pass by' means either 'to let someone through' or 'to miss, skip'.

history.meaning: to let pass; to miss, skip

проработать.etymology: Formed with prefix про- ('for a certain duration; thoroughly') from работать ('to work'), derived from работа ('work'), from Proto-Slavic *orbota.

history.meaning: to work (for a time); to work through thoroughly

прорваться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of прорвать ('to tear through, breach'), formed with prefix про- ('through') from рвать ('to tear, rend'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *rъvati.

history.meaning: to break through, to pull through

просить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic просити ('to ask, beg, request'), from Proto-Slavic *prositi, continuing the Proto-Indo-European root *preḱ- ('to ask, entreat'), cognate with Latin precārī ('to pray, entreat'), German fragen ('to ask'), and Lithuanian prašyti ('to ask').

проследить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') and следить ('to track, watch, keep an eye on'), derived from след ('footprint, track', from Proto-Slavic *slědъ).

history.meaning: to track down; to see to it, make sure

простить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic простити ('to set free, release from debt or guilt, forgive'), from Proto-Slavic *prostiti, a denominative verb from *prostъ ('free, straight, unencumbered, simple', modern Russian простой). Literally 'to make someone free of an obligation'.
простить.notes: The imperative **Простите!** ('Forgive me! / Excuse me!') is slightly weightier and more deferential than **Извините!**.

просто.etymology: Adverb and particle formed from the short neuter singular of простой ('simple, plain, straight'), from Old East Slavic простъ ('straight, upright, simple, free'), from Proto-Slavic *prostъ (literally 'standing forward, straight', from *pro- 'forward' + *stati 'to stand').

простоватый.etymology: Attenuative adjective formed with suffix -оватый ('somewhat, rather') from простой ('simple, plain'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *prostъ ('straight, simple, free').

просторно.etymology: Adverb formed from просторный ('spacious, roomy'), derived from простор ('open space, expanse'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *pro-storъ ('wide open space', from *sterti 'to spread, extend').

простыня.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic простыня ('plain unsewn length of linen cloth, bedsheet'), derived from простой ('simple, plain, unornamented', from Proto-Slavic *prostъ) with the feminine noun suffix -ыня: originally 'a plain, simple sheet of linen cloth' as opposed to tailored or embroidered garments.

просыпаться.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of проснуться ('to wake up'), formed from the prefix про- ('through, out of') and the iterative stem -сыпать (with lengthened zero-grade vowel ы < *ū from the root of спать 'to sleep', Old East Slavic съпати, Proto-Slavic *sъpati, from PIE *swep- 'to sleep').

против.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic противу / противъ ('against, opposite, facing'), from Proto-Slavic *protivъ, derived from the prefix *proti / *proty ('towards, facing, against'; compare Ancient Greek προτί / πρός and Sanskrit práti).

противень.etymology: A folk-etymological reshaping of German Bratpfanne 'roasting pan' (braten 'to roast' + Pfanne 'pan'). Because Bratpfanne was unfamiliar to Russian ears, speakers adapted its beginning toward the native word против.
противень.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel е in oblique cases: противень -> на противне.

противник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic противьникъ ('adversary, enemy'), formed with agent suffix -ник from противный ('opposite, opposing'), from против ('against, opposite', Proto-Slavic *protivъ).

профессионал.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century via French professionnel / English professional, derived from Medieval Latin professiōnālis and Classical Latin professiō ('public declaration, occupation, profession', from profitērī 'to declare openly').

профессия.etymology: Borrowed via German Profession, Polish profesja, or French profession from Latin professiō ('public declaration, occupation, profession'), from profitērī ('to declare openly, profess').

профессор.etymology: Borrowed via German Professor from Latin professor ('public teacher, one who professes an art or science'), an agent noun from profitērī ('to declare openly, profess', from pro- 'forth' + fatērī 'to acknowledge, speak').

профилактика.etymology: Learned medical/technical borrowing via German Prophylaktik / French prophylactique from Ancient Greek προφυλακτικός (prophulaktikós, 'precautionary, guarding beforehand'), from προφυλάσσω ('to keep guard before').

прохлаждаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of прохлаждать ('to cool, refresh'), borrowed with Old Church Slavonic non-pleophonic -хлад- (compare native прохолодиться) from про- + хладъ ('coolness', Proto-Slavic *xoldъ), shifting from 'to take one's ease in the cool shade' to 'to idle, loaf'.

history.meaning: to cool oneself, refresh oneself, take leisure

проход.etymology: Deverbal noun from проходить ('to walk through, pass'), formed from prefix про- ('through') + ход ('going, passage', from Proto-Slavic *xodъ).

проходить.etymology: Formed from the prefix про- ('through, past') + ходить ('to walk, go', from Proto-Slavic *xoditi). Means both 'to walk through, pass by' and, in hospitality (Проходите, пожалуйста!), 'to come on in (through the doorway)'.

history.meaning: to come in, pass through, elapse

прочий.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic прочии ('remaining, other'), derived from the archaic adverb прочь / проче ('away, beyond, further on'), from Proto-Slavic *pročь, formed from the Indo-European root *pro- ('forward, forth, away'; compare Latin procul 'far off' and Russian про-). Originally meaning 'that which lies further on, the rest', it became the adjective for 'other, remaining'.

history.meaning: other, remaining (esp. in и прочее 'et cetera')

прочитать.etymology: Formed as the perfective of читать ('to read') by adding the prefix про- ('through from start to finish'). The base verb читать comes from Old East Slavic читати (iterative of чисти / чьту, Proto-Slavic *čьtǫ, *čisti 'to count, reckon, read, honour').

прочность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость formed from прочный ('durable, solid, lasting'), derived from прок ('benefit, reserve for the future, durability', originally 'what remains over/ahead', from Proto-Slavic *prokъ).

прочный.etymology: Derived with suffix -ный from прок ('lasting use, benefit for the future', as in впрок), inherited from Old East Slavic прокъ ('remainder, future'), from Proto-Slavic *prokъ ('remaining, further', from *pro).

прошлое.etymology: Substantivized neuter singular of прошлый ('past, bygone'), contracted from прошедший / прошъдъшии, past active participle of пройти ('to pass, go by'), from про- + идти (stem шьд-, Proto-Slavic *pro-šьdlъ).

прощать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прощати (imperfective of простити 'to pardon, forgive, set free', with щ < *stj; compare native East Slavic простить), from Proto-Slavic *prostiti (from *prostъ 'free, straight, simple').

прощение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прощение ('release, pardon, forgiveness'), the verbal noun of простити / простить ('to forgive, release, set free'), derived from простъ ('simple, straight, free', Russian простой). The -щ- reflects the Old Church Slavonic outcome of Proto-Slavic *stj.

history.meaning: free, simple → to set free, pardon

прощение.notes: Common in the polite apology **Прошу прощения** ('I beg your pardon / excuse me').

проявить.etymology: Formed with prefix про- ('forth, out') from явить ('to show, reveal, manifest'), inherited from Old East Slavic явити, from Proto-Slavic *aviti ('to make clear, reveal').

history.meaning: to show, display, manifest; to develop (film)

прямо.etymology: Adverb formed from the short neuter of прямой ('straight, direct'), from Old East Slavic прямъ ('straight, upright, frank'), from Proto-Slavic *prěmъ. Used both spatially ('straight ahead') and as an emphatic particle ('right, directly').

прямой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic прямыи ('straight, direct, upright, frank'), from Proto-Slavic *prěmъ ('straight, direct').

прятать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic прятати ('to put away, tidy, bury, hide'), from Proto-Slavic *prętati ('to gather up, stow away, conceal'; compare Czech zpřátat 'to tidy away' and Slovene sprátati 'to clear away, store'). From 'clearing things away into storage', in Russian it became the standard verb for 'to hide, conceal'.

history.meaning: to stow away, put in order
to stow away, prepare for burial, conceal

прятки.etymology: Plural noun derived from прятать ('to hide, conceal'), inherited from Old East Slavic прятати ('to put away, tidy, bury, hide'), from Proto-Slavic *prętati.

психовать.etymology: 20th-century colloquial verb formed with suffix -овать from псих ('hothead, neurotic person; fit of temper'), a back-formation/clipping from психопат or психический (from Ancient Greek ψυχή psukhḗ 'soul, mind').

психология.etymology: Borrowed via German Psychologie / French psychologie from New Latin psychologia, coined in the 16th century from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, 'soul, mind') + -λογία (-logía, 'study, discourse').

публика.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish publika or German Publikum / French public from Latin pūblica (rēs) / pūblicus ('pertaining to the people, public', from populus 'people').

пугать.etymology: Imperfective verb (paired with напугать / испугать 'to frighten, scare'). Attested in East Slavic (compare dialectal пуга 'whip; owl', Ukrainian пугач 'eagle owl'), generally considered by Vasmer to be of expressive or onomatopoeic origin (from the hooting or sudden cry *pug- used to startle birds or animals, or from the crack of a whip).

пустой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пустъ / пустыи ('empty, deserted, uninhabited'), from Proto-Slavic *pustъ, closely cognate with Old Prussian pausto ('wild').

пустяк.etymology: Formed in Russian with the expressive noun suffix -як from пустой ('empty, hollow, vain, trivial', from Old East Slavic пустыи and Proto-Slavic *pustъ): literally 'an empty, inconsequential thing, a trifle'.
пустяк.notes: In the plural, *Пустяки!* means 'It's nothing!, Don't mention it!, A mere trifle!'.

путать.etymology: Derived from путо / пута ('fetters, hobbles for a horse's legs, bonds'), inherited from Old East Slavic путо, from Proto-Slavic *pǫto ('fetter, snare, cord', related to пнуть / пядь).

history.meaning: to tangle; to confuse, mix up

путеводитель.etymology: A native compound of путь 'way, road' and водитель 'one who leads', joined by the linking vowel -е-: literally 'a way-leader'. It names a guidebook, and in older usage also a guide.

путь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic путь and Proto-Slavic *pǫtь 'way, road, journey', from Proto-Indo-European *pontohs 'crossing, path', cognate with Latin pons ('bridge') and Sanskrit pantha ('road, path').
путь.notes: Unique masculine noun in Russian: it is masculine (добрый путь!), yet declines like a feminine -ь noun except in the instrumental singular (путём).

путёвка.etymology: Noun in -ка formed from путёвый / путевой ('relating to a road, journey, or dispatch'), derived from путь ('way, road, journey'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *pǫtь ('path, way').

пушистый.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -истый from пух ('down, fluff, soft fur'), inherited from Old East Slavic пухъ, from Proto-Slavic *puxъ ('breath, puff, soft down', of onomatopoeic origin).

пчелиный.etymology: Possessive/relational adjective formed with the animal suffix -иный from пчела ('bee'), inherited from Old East Slavic бъчела and Proto-Slavic *bъčela ('bee', an expressive root connected with buzzing).

пытать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пытати ('to ask, inquire, investigate, test; to interrogate under torture'), from Proto-Slavic *pytati ('to inquire, search into, probe'). While its reflexive derivative пытаться kept the mild sense 'to try, attempt' (and Ukrainian питати means simply 'to ask'), non-reflexive пытать in Russian specialized in legal history (from judicial interrogation on the rack) to mean 'to torture'.

history.meaning: to ask, investigate; to question under torture

пытаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of пытать ('to test, try, question'), inherited from Old East Slavic пытати ('to ask, investigate, strive') and Proto-Slavic *pytati.

history.meaning: to test → to try, attempt, endeavour

пьянка.etymology: Colloquial noun in -ка formed from пьяный ('drunk, intoxicated'), inherited from Old East Slavic пияныи / пьяныи, from Proto-Slavic *pьjanъ ('drunk', old participle from *piti 'to drink').

пьянство.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пияньство, formed with abstract suffix -ство from пьяный ('drunk'), from Proto-Slavic *pьjanъ (from *piti 'to drink').

пьяный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пияныи ('drunk, intoxicated'), from Proto-Slavic *pьjanъ, historically an archaic passive/stative participle in *-nъ formed from *piti ('to drink', Russian пить; compare Sanskrit pīyáte 'is drunk'), meaning 'having drunk deeply'.

пятница.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пятница (Old Church Slavonic пѧтьница), formed from пятый / пять ('fifth / five'). Slavic weekday names count cleanly from Monday: вторник (2nd), среда (middle), четверг (4th), пятница (5th).

пятно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пятно ('brand mark, scar, spot'), from Proto-Slavic *pętьno ('mark, stamp, spot'), connected by Vasmer either with *pęta ('heel, footprint impression') or *pęti ('to stretch, strike, brand').

пять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пять (Old Church Slavonic пѧть), from Proto-Slavic *pętь ('five', originally a feminine abstract noun 'a group of five'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe ('five'), cognate with English five, German fünf, Ancient Greek πέντε, and Sanskrit páñca.

пятьдесят.etymology: Compound numeral inherited from Old East Slavic пять десятъ ('five tens, fifty'), from Proto-Slavic *pętь desętъ, where пять ('five') governed the archaic genitive plural десятъ ('of tens', from десять 'ten').

пёсик.etymology: Diminutive in -ик of пёс ('dog, hound'), inherited from Old East Slavic пьсъ, from Proto-Slavic *pьsъ ('dog').

работа.etymology: The older Russian form робота could mean work, servitude or bondage. Vasmer connects it with the same historical family as раб, a slave. The everyday modern meaning is work; the older senses explain a history of compelled labour.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: работа

работа.notes:
- Collocations: *найти работу* (find a job), *уйти с работы* (leave work), *на работе* (at work).
- *За работу!* is an idiomatic call to get started.

работать.etymology: Denominative verb built on работа ('work, labour'), generalizing the South Slavic / Church Slavonic initial ра- (compare Old East Slavic роботати and Czech pracovat / robotovat), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *orbota ('hard labour').

работящий.etymology: Colloquial adjective formed on the participial pattern -ящий from работать ('to work'), derived from работа ('work, labor'), from Proto-Slavic *orbota.

рабочий.etymology: Derived from работа ('work, labor', Old Russian робота) with palatalization of т > ч before the adjectival suffix -ий (compare Old Church Slavonic работии / рабочии). Functions both as an relational adjective ('working, work-related') and as a substantivized noun ('worker, laborer').

равнодушный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic равьнодушьнъ (originally 'unanimous, of like mind', calquing Greek ἰσόψυχος, from равный 'equal, even' + душа 'soul'; later reinterpreted after French indifférent / German gleichgültig as 'even-minded, unmoved, indifferent').

history.meaning: of equal spirit; later unmoved, indifferent

равномерно.etymology: Adverb formed from равномерный ('uniform, even-measured'), compound of равный ('equal', Old Church Slavonic равьнъ) + мера ('measure', Proto-Slavic *měra).

равный.etymology: Borrowed with Old Church Slavonic initial ра- (compare native East Slavic ровный 'flat, even') from равьнъ ('flat, level, equal'), from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ ('level, even').

ради.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ради and Old Church Slavonic ради ('for the sake of, on account of'), from Proto-Slavic *radi, an old locative/instrumental case form connected with *radъ ('glad, willing, caring for', modern рад) and Old Persian rādiy ('on account of, for the sake of').

history.meaning: for the sake of, because of
for the sake of (governs the genitive case)

радостный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic радостьныи, formed with suffix -ный from радость ('joy, gladness'), derived from рад ('glad'), from Proto-Slavic *radostь.

раз.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic разъ ('stroke, blow; one time, occasion'), from Proto-Slavic *razъ, an o-grade noun derived from *rězati ('to cut, strike', modern Russian резать). Just as French coup and German Schlag shifted from 'a strike' to 'one time', a single stroke of counting became Russian раз ('time, occasion; one!').

разбивать.etymology: Imperfective of разбить ('to smash, break to pieces'), formed with prefix раз- ('apart, into pieces') from бивать / бить ('to beat, strike', from Proto-Slavic *biti).

разбирать.etymology: Imperfective of разобрать ('to take apart, sort out, take one by one'), formed with prefix раз- ('apart') and lengthened-grade iterative stem -бирать from брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

history.meaning: to take apart; to take, grab (one each); to sort out

разбить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic разбитии, formed from the prefix раз- ('apart, into pieces') and бить ('to beat, strike', Old East Slavic бити, Proto-Slavic *biti). Literally, 'to strike into pieces, smash, shatter'.

history.meaning: to break, smash, shatter; to wreck (a car)

разбрасываться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective formed with prefix раз- ('in all directions, wastefully') and -ся from брасывать / бросать ('to throw, fling'), from Proto-Slavic *brosati.

разваливаться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective of развалиться ('to collapse, fall apart, sprawl'), formed with prefix раз- ('apart') and -ся from валить ('to topple, tumble'), from Proto-Slavic *valiti.

разведка.etymology: Noun in -ка formed from разведать ('to find out, explore, reconnoiter'), derived from раз- + ведать ('to know, inquire'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *vědati ('to know').

разведённый.etymology: Past passive participle of развести ('to lead apart, separate, divorce; to dilute'), formed from раз- ('apart') + вести ('to lead', from Proto-Slavic *vesti).

развернуть.etymology: Formed with the prefix раз- ('apart, un-') + вернуть ('to turn, roll', from Proto-Slavic *vьrnǫti / *vьrtěti 'to turn'): 'to unroll, unfold, unwrap'.

развесить.etymology: Formed with the distributive prefix раз- ('around, in various places') + весить ('to hang', causative of висеть 'to be hanging', from Proto-Slavic *věsiti).

history.meaning: to hang up around, string out

развлекаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of развлекать ('to divert, entertain', originally 'to draw/pull apart [one's thoughts from care]', calquing French distraire / divertir), built on Old Church Slavonic развлѣщи (from *velkti 'to draw, drag').

развод.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from разводить / развести ('to lead apart, separate; to dissolve a marriage; to breed; in slang, to string someone along / con'), built from раз- ('apart') + водить ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *voditi). Literally 'a leading apart', whence 'divorce' (and in modern colloquial slang, 'a scam, con, hustle').

history.meaning: leading apart, separation → divorce; (slang) scam, con

развязать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix раз- ('apart, un-') and вязать ('to tie, bind, knot', inherited from Old East Slavic вязати, Proto-Slavic *vęzati). Means literally 'to untie, unbind' and figuratively 'to unleash, start (a war or quarrel): развязать войну'.

history.meaning: to untie, unknot; to unleash (a conflict)

развязывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the secondary imperfectivizing suffix -ывать from развязать ('to untie, unfasten'), built on prefix раз- ('apart, un-') + вязать ('to tie, bind', from Proto-Slavic *vęzati).

разгадать.etymology: Formed with the prefix раз- ('apart, unravelling') + гадать ('to guess, divine, ponder'), inherited from Old East Slavic гадати and Proto-Slavic *gadati ('to suppose, divine, speak').

history.meaning: to solve, figure out (a riddle, mystery, or code)

разгладиться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form in -ся of разгладить ('to smooth out, iron flat'), formed with prefix раз- ('out flat') + гладить ('to smooth, stroke, iron', from гладкий 'smooth', Proto-Slavic *gladъkъ).

history.meaning: to smooth out → to smooth out, unpucker (of a wrinkled brow or cloth)

разгромный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from разгром ('utter rout, devastation'), deverbal noun from разгромить ('to smash, rout'), from раз- + громить ('to smash, thunder against'), derived from гром ('thunder', Proto-Slavic *gromъ).

раздеваться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of раздевать ('to undress'), imperfective of раздеть, formed with prefix раз- ('un-, apart', by antonymic analogy with одеть 'to dress') from деть ('to put', Proto-Slavic *děti).

history.meaning: to take off one's coat; to undress

разделение.etymology: Verbal noun from разделить ('to divide, separate'), inherited from Old Church Slavonic раздѣление, from раз- ('apart') + дѣлити ('to divide, share', Proto-Slavic *děliti).

разделить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic раздѣлити ('to divide, part, distribute'), formed with prefix раз- ('apart, into parts') + делить ('to divide, share', from Proto-Slavic *děliti, related to *dělъ 'part, share').

разделывать.etymology: Imperfective of разделать ('to dress/butcher a carcass, finish off, prepare'), formed with prefix раз- ('apart') from делать ('to do, make, work on'), from Proto-Slavic *dělati.

раздельно.etymology: Adverb formed from раздельный ('separate, distinct'), derived from разделить ('to divide apart'), from раз- + делить ('to divide', Proto-Slavic *děliti).

раздумывать.etymology: Imperfective of раздумать ('to ponder, deliberate; to change one's mind'), formed with prefix раз- from думать ('to think'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *dumati.

разливать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from разлить ('to pour out into vessels; to spill'), built on prefix раз- ('out, into several containers') + ливать (iterative of лить 'to pour', from Proto-Slavic *liti).

history.meaning: to pour out (tea, soup into cups/bowls); to spill

разлить.etymology: Formed with prefix раз- ('out, apart, into vessels') from лить ('to pour'), inherited from Old East Slavic лити (лию), from Proto-Slavic *liti ('to pour').

размер.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from размерить ('to measure out, proportion'), built from prefix раз- ('out, apart') + мерить / мера ('to measure / measure', from Proto-Slavic *měra, from PIE *meh₁- 'to measure').

history.meaning: to measure out → size, dimension, meter

разминаться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective of размяться ('to stretch one's limbs, warm up'), formed with prefix раз- from мять (мну, iterative -минать, 'to knead, rub, limber up'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *męti ('to knead, press').

history.meaning: to knead, press, work until supple
to warm up, to limber up

размытый.etymology: Past passive participle of размыть ('to wash out, blur with water'), formed from prefix раз- + мыть ('to wash', from Proto-Slavic *myti).

history.meaning: to wash out → blurred, washed-out, smudged

размыть.etymology: Formed with the prefix раз- ('apart, dissolving') + мыть ('to wash', inherited from Old East Slavic мыти and Proto-Slavic *myti): 'to wash away, erode with water, blur ink or paint'.

history.meaning: to wash out, blur (with water or moisture)

разнервничаться.etymology: Inceptive/intensive reflexive formed with circumfix раз-...-ся from нервничать ('to be nervous, fret'), derived from нервный / нерв ('nerve', borrowed via German Nerv / French nerf from Latin nervus 'sinew, nerve').

history.meaning: to get worked up, to get all nervous

разный.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic prefix vocalism раз- (alongside older native розный) from Old Church Slavonic разьнъ ('divided, separate, different'), built on the prefix/preposition *orz- ('apart, asunder', related to резать 'to cut') + adjectival suffix -ный.

разобрать.etymology: Formed with prefix разо- ('apart') from брать ('to take'), inherited from Old East Slavic бърати, from Proto-Slavic *bьrati ('to take, gather').

history.meaning: to take apart, to dismantle; to sort out

разобраться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from разобрать ('to take apart, sort out, dismantle'), built from раз- / разо- ('apart') + брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati). From the concrete sense of 'sorting items out one by one', it developed the figurative sense 'to figure out, understand thoroughly, settle a matter'.

history.meaning: to sort out → to figure out, get to the bottom of

разогревать.etymology: Imperfective of разогреть ('to warm up, reheat'), formed with prefix разо- ('thoroughly, up') from греть ('to warm, heat'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěti.

разозлить.etymology: Perfective formed with intensive prefix разо- from злить ('to anger, make mad'), derived from злой ('angry, wicked, evil'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъlъ.

разок-другой.etymology: Colloquial compound adverbial phrase formed from разок (diminutive in -ок of раз 'time, occasion', from Proto-Slavic *razъ 'stroke, time') + другой ('another, a second', from Proto-Slavic *drugъ).

разорвать.etymology: Formed with the prefix разо- ('apart, in pieces') + рвать ('to tear, rip, rend'), inherited from Old East Slavic ръвати and Proto-Slavic *rъvati ('to tear, pluck').

history.meaning: to tear in two, tear up

разорить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic разорити ('to destroy, demolish, lay waste'), formed from раз- ('apart') + орити ('to tear down, overthrow, destroy', Proto-Slavic *oriti).

history.meaning: to ruin, to bankrupt, lay waste

разочарование.etymology: Verbal noun from разочаровать ('to disenchant, disappoint'), formed as a calque on French désenchantement / German Enttäuschung from раз- ('un-') + очарование ('enchantment, charm', from чары 'magic, sorcery').

разочаровать.etymology: Formed with reversative prefix раз- ('un-, dis-') from очаровать ('to charm, enchant', derived from чары 'magic, spell', Proto-Slavic *čarъ), calquing French désenchanter ('to break a spell, disillusion').

разрешать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разрѣшати (imperfective of разрѣшити 'to untie, loosen, absolve, permit'), from раз- ('apart, un-') + рѣшити ('to untie, solve', Proto-Slavic *rěšiti).

history.meaning: to untie, release from a bond, permit

разрешить.etymology: Borrowed from Church Slavonic разрѣшити ('to untie, unbind, absolve, release from a prohibition'), formed from prefix раз- ('un-, apart') + рѣшити ('to untie a knot, loosen, solve', from Proto-Slavic *rěšiti): literally 'to untie a restriction', hence 'to allow, permit' and 'to resolve'.

разрешиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of разрешить ('to untie, resolve, settle'), from Old Church Slavonic разрѣшити ('to untie, loosen', from Proto-Slavic *rěšiti).

history.meaning: to be resolved, to work itself out

разрушить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix раз- ('apart, into pieces') and рушить ('to pull down, demolish, shatter'), inherited from Old East Slavic рушити and Proto-Slavic *rušiti ('to tear apart, break up, set in motion', cognate with Lithuanian raũšti 'to dig up, tear').

разумный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic разумьныи ('endowed with reason, wise, sensible'), derived from разум ('reason, intellect'), from раз- + ум ('mind, intellect', Proto-Slavic *umъ).

разыграть.etymology: Formed with prefix раз- ('out, thoroughly') from играть ('to play, act'), inherited from Old East Slavic играти, from Proto-Slavic *jьgrati ('to play').

history.meaning: to play a prank on; to act out; to raffle

рак.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ракъ ('crayfish; cancer'), from Proto-Slavic *rakъ ('crayfish, crab'); the medical sense 'cancer' is an ancient calque on Latin cancer / Greek καρκίνος ('crab; malignant tumor', after the crab-like swollen veins around a tumor).

рамка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of рама ('frame, window frame'), borrowed via Polish rama from Middle High German rame / German Rahmen ('frame, border, support').

ранний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рании ('early'), adjective formed from рано ('early, in the morning'), from Proto-Slavic *ranъ ('early').

раскатать.etymology: Formed with prefix рас- ('out, flat') from катать ('to roll'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *katati ('to roll').

history.meaning: to roll out flat; (colloq.) to crush, to steamroll

раскручивать.etymology: Imperfective of раскрутить ('to untwist, unscrew, spin up; in slang, to promote'), formed with prefix рас- ('un-; into full motion') from крутить ('to twist, turn, spin', from Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti).

history.meaning: to unscrew, take apart; (colloq.) to promote

раскрываться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form in -ся of раскрывать ('to open wide, uncover'), formed from prefix рас- ('apart, wide') + крывать (iterative of крыть 'to cover', from Proto-Slavic *kryti).

history.meaning: to uncover, open wide → to open up, fall open (of a book, flower, or door)

распахнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb formed with prefix рас- ('wide apart') + пахнуть ('to sweep, wave, fling', from older Russian пахать 'to sweep, fan, wave', distinct from пахнуть 'to smell'). Literally 'to fling wide open with a sweeping motion'.

history.meaning: to throw open, fling wide (doors, windows, or coat lapels)

расписной.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ной from расписать ('to paint with decorative patterns'), built on prefix рас- ('all over, out') + писать ('to paint, write', from Proto-Slavic *pьsati, originally 'to adorn with colour or incisions').

history.meaning: to decorate with paint → painted, hand-decorated

расплакаться.etymology: Inceptive/intensive reflexive formed with circumfix рас-...-ся from плакать ('to weep, cry'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *plakati ('to weep').

history.meaning: to burst into tears, start crying

распределять.etymology: Imperfective of распределить ('to distribute, allocate, apportion'), formed in bookish Russian from рас- ('apart') + предел ('boundary, limit, allotted share', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдѣлъ, from *děliti 'to divide').

распробовать.etymology: Formed with prefix рас- ('thoroughly, fully') from пробовать ('to try, taste, test'), borrowed via Polish próbować and Middle High German prōben from Latin probāre ('to test, approve').

распугать.etymology: Formed with prefix рас- ('in all directions, away') from пугать ('to frighten, scare'), of expressive East Slavic origin (related to пужать).

рассказывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of рассказать ('to tell, narrate, recount'), formed from the prefix раз- / рас- ('out, in detail') + сказывать / сказать ('to say, tell', from Proto-Slavic *kazati 'to show, point out, speak').

расслабить.etymology: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic раслабити ('to loosen, weaken, relax'), formed with prefix рас- from слабить ('to make weak/loose'), derived from слабый ('weak, slack', Proto-Slavic *slabъ).

расслаблять.etymology: Imperfective of расслабить ('to relax, loosen'), formed from рас- + слабый ('slack, loose, weak', inherited from Proto-Slavic *slabъ).

расслабляться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of расслаблять ('to relax, loosen up'), derived from рас- + слабый ('slack, loose, weak', from Proto-Slavic *slabъ).

расследование.etymology: Verbal noun from расследовать ('to investigate, inquire into'), formed with prefix рас- ('thoroughly') from следовать ('to follow a track, examine'), derived from след ('footprint, track, trace', Proto-Slavic *slědъ).

расстраиваться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb (paired with расстроиться) formed from расстраивать / расстроить ('to throw out of order; to detune a musical instrument; to upset'), built from раз- / рас- ('apart, out of order') + строить ('to arrange, tune, build', Proto-Slavic *strojiti). Just as настроение ('mood') comes from tuning an instrument, расстраиваться means 'to become out of tune emotionally, get upset or distressed'.

history.meaning: to come out of tune → to get upset, feel distressed

расстроить.etymology: Formed with reversative prefix рас- ('out of order, apart') from строить ('to tune an instrument, arrange in order, build'), derived from строй ('order, harmony, tuning', Proto-Slavic *strojь), shifting from 'to put out of tune/order' to 'to upset emotionally'.

history.meaning: to put in order, tune, arrange
to put out of tune, disrupt; to upset, distress
